title: Tutorial
text:
This tutorial takes you through the main DeepAcoustics workflow using real data: viewing annotated calls, training a detection network, testing how well a network performs, and running a network on new audio. Each exercise builds on the pages in this guide, which are linked throughout for more detail.


The Tutorial Data
The tutorial uses a multiclass baleen whale dataset of blue whale A and B calls and fin whale 18 Hz and 20 Hz pulses. The training and test data were recorded on Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI) hydrophones off Newport, Oregon, and the deployment data come from the SanctSound monitoring site MB01 in Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary. All audio has a sampling rate of 400 Hz (a bandwidth of 0 to 200 Hz).
The tutorial data are a small subset of a larger Dryad repository, which contains the full annotated training and evaluation datasets and the networks from a recent multiclass baleen whale effort:

Annotated training and evaluation data and DeepAcoustics-derived networks for multi-class baleen whale calls (doi: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.x0k6djj2d)

Data Sources:

NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries, and US Navy (2021). Humpback Whale Sound Production Recorded at SanctSound Site MB01_06, SanctSound Data Products. NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. (Accessed 18 February 2026).
NSF Ocean Observatories Initiative (n.d.). Coastal Endurance Array, Oregon Offshore and Oregon Shelf Cabled Benthic Experiment Packages, Broadband Hydrophone (CE04OSBP-LJ01C-11-HYDBBA105; CE02SHBP-LJ01D-11-HYDBBA106) data. OOI Raw Data Archive. https://rawdata.oceanobservatories.org/files/. Accessed 2020.


Downloading the data
Download the tutorial_data folder from the DeepAcoustics Guide and Tutorial GitHub repository. Save it somewhere easy to find, such as your Documents folder, and keep the folder structure as it is.


What’s in the folder

Network_Settings_Template.xlsx: a spreadsheet template for keeping track of the settings and results of each network you train (see Tracking your networks).
OOI_Multiclass: the data for the exercises.

01_Training

01_Training_Audio: five folders of training audio (5-minute .wav files), each with its Raven selection table, and the five matching annotations files (_Annotations.mat) already imported into DeepAcoustics.
02_Images: an empty folder for saving your training images.

02_Networks

tiny_YOLO: a trained Tiny YOLO network (TinyYOLO.mat) to test, and a Detections_and_Performance folder for saving the test results.

03_Testing

01_OOI_2017_Feb_03: 49 test audio files from 3 February 2017 and their Raven selection table.
HYDDBA105OOI_20170203_Test_Detections.mat: the test annotations, already imported into DeepAcoustics. This is the ground-truth file for testing a network.

04_Annotation_Summary.pdf: the metadata document from the Dryad submission, describing how the calls in the training and test files were annotated. It explains the decisions that went into the annotation process, including the criteria for each call type, with example spectrograms. Read it to help interpret the annotations, for example why some faint calls were boxed and others were not.
05_Deployment_Call_Review

Network: a trained multiclass network (Pacific_LF_tinyYOLO_2026_v1.mat) for detecting calls in new audio.
SanctSound_MB01: 24 audio files from SanctSound site MB01, each about 6 hours long.









ImportantKeep a backup of the tutorial data



Some steps write changes into the detections files (for example, adding noise when creating training images, or adding the date and time). Keep an unchanged copy of the tutorial_data folder, or download it again, if you want to start an exercise over.




Tracking your networks
As you train and test networks, it quickly becomes hard to remember which settings produced which results. Network_Settings_Template.xlsx has one row per network version and columns for:

Training details: the network, call types (classes), image size, image duration, anchor boxes, solver, learning rate, mini-batch size, epochs, validation split, time to train, and the number of training images and noise samples.
Test results: for each test file, the true positives, false positives, false negatives, precision, recall, F-score, average precision, and mAP.

Fill in a row each time you train or test a network in the exercises below.




Exercise 1: Viewing Annotated Data
In this exercise, you open the test annotations, adjust the display so the calls are easy to see, and move through the calls. See Importing Data and Annotation Review for more detail.

Set the audio folder. Go to File > Select Audio Folder and select OOI_Multiclass > 03_Testing > 01_OOI_2017_Feb_03.
Load the test annotations. Go to File > Load Detections and select 03_Testing > HYDDBA105OOI_20170203_Test_Detections.mat.

The file contains four call types: 18 Hz, 20 Hz, A, and B. Click Select all and then OK.
If DeepAcoustics cannot find the audio, it asks you to select the folder containing the audio files. Select 01_OOI_2017_Feb_03.

Choose a starting audio file. Select the first audio file (HYDDBA105OOI_20170203-020000.wav) and click OK.
Adjust the display settings. Select Display Settings and enter:

Frequency Lower Limit (Hz): 0
Frequency Upper Limit (Hz): 200 (half of the 400 Hz sampling rate)
Units of Spectrogram Parameters: Samples
Window Size: 256
Overlap (%): 80 to 90
NFFT: 256
Click OK. The spectrograms are redrawn with the new settings.

Adjust the Focus and Page durations.

Page: set to 300 seconds, the full length of each audio file, so the lower panel shows the whole file and where all of its calls fall.
Focus: set to 120 seconds. This suits blue and fin whale calls: it is long enough to show whole blue whale B calls, which can last up to about 20 seconds, along with a series of fin whale pulses. Shorten it to look closely at individual fin whale pulses.
These are suggestions; adjust both to whatever works best for you.

Adjust the color limits and color map.

Use + and - beside Low Color Limit and High Color Limit until the calls stand out clearly from the background noise.
Try a different Color Map to see which makes the calls easiest to see.
Check that you can see the calls and their boxes in both the upper (focus) and lower (page) panels.

Move from call to call. Use the Navigation panel at the bottom of the window to step through the calls.

Move to the next or previous call, and notice how the call details on the left of the window update for each call.
Use the pink file buttons to move to the next audio file, or to the next audio file that contains a call.
Type a call number in the box at the top left of the window to jump straight to that call.
Select Play Call (or press p) to listen to a call. If it is hard to hear, go to File > Change Playback Rate.

Explore the call types. Use Filter Display to show only one call type at a time (for example, only A and B to see just the blue whale calls). Compare what you see with the examples and annotation criteria in 04_Annotation_Summary.pdf.







Tip



If you change anything and want to save the session, save it under a new file name so the original test annotations stay unchanged for Exercise 3.





Exercise 2: Training a Network
In this exercise, you create training images from the five training annotations files and train a network on them. See Creating Training Images and Network Training for a full explanation of each setting. The settings below are a good starting point, but the choice is up to you; the reference settings of the provided network are listed in Exercise 3.

Part A: Create the training images

Open the tool. Go to Tools > Network Training > Create Detection Network Training Images.
Select the training annotations. In 01_Training > 01_Training_Audio, select all five _Annotations.mat files and click Open.
Point each file to its audio. Because the files were created on another computer, DeepAcoustics asks you to Select folder containing each file’s audio. The folder names match the instrument and date (or name) in each annotations file:







Annotations file
Audio folder




HYDBBA106OOI_170105_Blue_Train_Annotations.mat
HYDBBA106_20170105_Blue


HYDBBA106OOI_170106_BlueFin_Train_Annotations.mat
HYDBBA106_20170106_BlueFin


HYDBBA106OOI_170120_Blue_Train_Annotations.mat
HYDBBA106_20170120_Blue


OOI_Train_A_Fin_Annotations.mat
OOI_Train_A_5minAudio_Fin


OOI_Train_B_Fin_Annotations.mat
OOI_Train_B_5minAudio_Fin




The dialog title names the audio file it is looking for, which tells you which folder to select.
If you select the wrong folder, DeepAcoustics stops with an error that the file was not found. Start again from step 1.

Choose the call types. For each file, click Select all and then OK.
Enter the training image settings. In the Settings for Training Images dialog, enter:

Units of Spectrogram Parameters: Samples
Low Frequency Cutoff (Hz): 0
High Frequency Cutoff (Hz): 200
Window Size: 256
Overlap (%): 80 to 90
NFFT: 256
Optimize: pressed in (on), so the image length is calculated for you. With 300-pixel images, this gives an image length of about 38.4 seconds at 80% overlap, or 19.2 seconds at 90% overlap.
Image Resolution (pixels): 300 (the default)
# of Augmented Duplicates: 0 to start
Randomly Add Noise: Yes. The annotations do not include noise, so DeepAcoustics adds noise examples automatically from the parts of the audio outside the call boxes.
Manually Select Validation Data: No. There are no separate validation files in this exercise; part of the training images will be set aside for validation when you train the network.
Click OK.

Select the output folder. Select 01_Training > 02_Images.
Review the summary and save the image table. When the images are done, read the summary of calls, split calls, and noise (see Understanding the summary), and save the image table (_Images.mat) in the 01_Training folder.

Do not move or rename the 02_Images folder afterward, because the image table stores the location of each image.




Part B: Train the network

Open the tool. Go to Tools > Network Training > Train Detection Network and select the image table you just saved.
Answer the setup questions.

Do you have Validation Image Tables, too? No
Train from existing network? No
Call Types Warning: check that the list shows 18 Hz, 20 Hz, A, B, and Noise, and click Yes.

Choose the training settings.

Base network: Tiny YOLO. It is the fastest to train; you can try the other architectures later.
Reduce image resolution? No, unless your GPU has crashed before.
Customize or Defaults: Customize.
Anchor boxes: select No so DeepAcoustics plots the mean IoU for 1 to 15 anchor boxes, and enter the number where the curve levels off (see Anchor boxes).
Solver: rmsprop, with an initial learning rate of 0.001.
Mini-batch size: 16 (Tiny YOLO can usually handle larger mini-batches, such as 64).
Maximum number of epochs: 10 is enough for a first try.
Use a proportion of the training data to validate? Yes, with a proportion of 0.2. Click Yes in the Check Proportions dialog.

Watch the training progress. Follow the training and validation loss in the Training Progress window (see Monitoring Training).
Save the network. Save the network in 02_Networks with a name that describes it, for example TinyYOLO_Tutorial_v1.mat.
Record your settings. Fill in a row in Network_Settings_Template.xlsx for this network.



Part C: Try other settings
Once you have trained one network, try changing one setting at a time, training again, and comparing the networks in Exercise 3. For example:

Augmented duplicates: add 1 or 2 augmented duplicates of each image, or leave them out.
Image resolution: try a smaller or larger image resolution.
Overlap: compare 80% and 90% overlap.
Architecture: try CSP-DarkNet-53 or ResNet-50.







NoteLarger settings need more computing power



This is a small training dataset, but more augmented duplicates, higher image resolutions, and larger architectures all increase the time, memory, and GPU resources needed to create images and train a network.






Exercise 3: Testing Network Performance
In this exercise, you test a network against the test annotations from Exercise 1. You can test the Tiny YOLO network provided in 02_Networks > tiny_YOLO, the network you trained in Exercise 2, or both. See Performance Testing for an explanation of each result.

Reference settings for the provided network
The network provided in 02_Networks > tiny_YOLO (TinyYOLO.mat) is the Pacific low-frequency (Pacific LF) multiclass network, the same network provided for Exercise 4. For reference, it was built with these settings:

Base network: Tiny YOLO (pre-trained), with a network input size of 320 × 320 pixels
Call types: 18 Hz, 20 Hz, 40-80 Hz, A, B, Bb, D, Noise, and UNID. The test file contains only 18 Hz, 20 Hz, A, and B.
Sampling rate: 400 Hz, with a frequency range of 0 to 200 Hz
Window Size and NFFT: 0.56 seconds (224 samples)
Overlap (%): 70
Image Length (s): 53.76 (optimized for 320-pixel images)
Anchor boxes: 10
Solver: rmsprop, with an initial learning rate of 0.0005
Mini-batch size: 64
Maximum number of epochs: 10
Validation: checked every 50 iterations; the saved network is the one with the lowest validation loss







ImportantThe provided network was trained on much more data



The Pacific LF network was trained on far more annotated data than the small training set in this tutorial, from several datasets and call types (see the Dryad repository). Use its settings and results as a reference point, but do not expect a network trained on the tutorial data alone to perform as well.




Running the test

Set the network folder. Go to File > Select Network Folder and select 02_Networks > tiny_YOLO (or 02_Networks, if you are testing your own network).
Open the tool. Go to Tools > Performance Metrics.
Select the ground-truth file. Select 03_Testing > HYDDBA105OOI_20170203_Test_Detections.mat.

If DeepAcoustics asks for the audio folder, select 03_Testing > 01_OOI_2017_Feb_03.

Choose the call types. Click Select all and then OK.
Select the network. Select TinyYOLO.mat (or your own network).
Enter the settings for running the network. Leave all three settings at 0 and click OK.
Let the network run. DeepAcoustics runs the network on all 49 test audio files.
Set the true positive threshold. Enter the IoU threshold a detection must reach to count as correct (see True Positive Threshold). Try 0.1 (detecting the call at all) and then run the test again with 0.5 (detecting the call moderately well) to see how the results change.
Review the results. Look at the precision-recall curve and P/R Result for each call type, and the confusion matrix (see Understanding the Results).

Which call types does the network detect well, and which are harder?
Which call types does it confuse with each other, or with noise?








NoteResults for call types that are not in the test file



DeepAcoustics reports results for every call type the network was trained on, not only those in the test file. The Pacific LF network is part of a larger effort to categorize more call types than are in the test file. It detects nine call types:

18 Hz and 20 Hz: fin whale pulses
40-80 Hz: fin whale 40 Hz pulses
A, B, and D: blue whale A, B, and D calls
Bb: sei whale downsweeps
UNID: a catch-all category for unidentified calls
Noise: background noise

The test file only contains annotations for 18 Hz, 20 Hz, A, and B. You will therefore see results and a confusion matrix row for 40-80 Hz, Bb, D, and UNID even though there are no annotated calls of those types to compare against. Any detections of those call types count as false positives here, so focus on the results for 18 Hz, 20 Hz, A, and B.



Save the results. Save the performance metrics file and the network’s detections in 02_Networks > tiny_YOLO > Detections_and_Performance.

Rename both files to include the test file, the network, and the IoU threshold, for example OOI_20170203_Test_TinyYOLO_IoU0.1_PerformanceMetrics.mat.

Record the results. Fill in the test results for this network in Network_Settings_Template.xlsx.
Look at the detections. Load the network’s detections file with File > Load Detections and step through them, as in Exercise 1, to see where the network did well and where it made mistakes.





Exercise 4: Deploying a Network on New Audio
In this exercise, you run a trained multiclass network on 24 audio files from SanctSound site MB01, add the date and time to the detections, and review them. See Network Deployment for more detail.

Part A: Detect calls

Set the audio folder. Go to File > Select Audio Folder and select 05_Deployment_Call_Review > SanctSound_MB01.
Set the network folder. Go to File > Select Network Folder and select 05_Deployment_Call_Review > Network.
Start detection. In the Detect, Load, & Record section, select Detect Calls.
Select the audio files. Select all 24 audio files.
Select the network. Select Pacific_LF_tinyYOLO_2026_v1.mat.
Select the output folder. Select 05_Deployment_Call_Review.
Enter the settings for running the network.

Total Analysis Length (Seconds; 0 = Full Duration): 0
Score Threshold (0-1): 0 keeps every detection. Try a higher value, such as 0.5, to keep only the more confident detections.
Append Date to FileName (1 = yes): 0, or 1 to add the date and time of the run to the file name.
Click OK.

Watch the progress. Each file is about 6 hours long, so this is about 144 hours of audio.

The progress bar shows the Detection Speed and the number of Call Fragments Found in each file.
The MATLAB Command Window shows the number of calls found in each file.

Find the detections file. DeepAcoustics saves the detections automatically in 05_Deployment_Call_Review. The file name starts with the first audio file’s name and ends with _24AudFiles_Detections.mat.



Part B: Add the date and time

Open the tool. Go to Tools > File Management > Add Date/Time.
Confirm the overwrite warning. Click Yes.
Select the detections file you created in Part A.

DeepAcoustics reads the start date and time of each audio file from its name. For example, SanctSound_MB01_06_671617061_201110004754.wav started on 2020-11-10 at 00:47:54.

Check the date and time. Drag the detections file into the MATLAB Command Window, double-click the Calls table in the Workspace panel, and scroll right to the StTime column to check that each call has a date and time.



Part C: Review the detections

Load the detections. Go to File > Load Detections, select the detections file, select all call types, and choose a starting audio file.
Adjust the display. Use the display settings from Exercise 1. Because these files are about 6 hours long, use a shorter Page duration (for example, 300 seconds) and move through each file page by page.
Review the calls. Accept correct detections (a), reject false positives (r), and relabel calls with the wrong call type (see Annotation Review).

To review many detections at once, use Tools > Call Review.

Save your review. Select Save Session and save the reviewed detections under a new file name.
Export to Raven (optional). With the reviewed detections loaded, go to File > Import/Export > Export to Raven and choose Selection Table to view the detections in Raven.

title: Network Training
text:
Once you have created your training images (see Creating Training Images), you can train a detection network. This page walks through each dialog in the training process and explains the settings. The architectures, hyperparameters, and anchor boxes referred to here are described in more detail in Architectures, Hyperparameters & Metrics.


Starting Training

Open the tool. Go to Tools > Network Training > Train Detection Network.
Select the image table(s). DeepAcoustics asks you to select the image table(s) (_Images.mat) for training. You can select more than one, for example to combine image tables made from different datasets, but they must all be in the same folder. It is usually easiest to keep your detections files in one folder, create an image table from them, and save any later image tables in that same folder. In this example, we select the image table created on the previous page.
Add validation image tables (if you have them). DeepAcoustics asks Do you have Validation Image Tables, too?

Yes: select the validation image table(s) (_ValImages.mat). You will only have these if you set Manually Select Validation Data to Yes when creating the training images. The validation tables must contain the same call types as the training tables.
No: continue without them. You will have the option to set aside a portion of your training data for validation later on. In this example, we select No.

Choose whether to build on an existing network. DeepAcoustics asks Train from existing network?

No: train a new network from scratch. Select No. This is the option to use for now.
Yes and Yes - TensorFlow: build on an existing DeepAcoustics network or a TensorFlow model. These options are still being developed and improved, so we do not recommend them at this time.

Confirm the call types. A Call Types Warning lists the call types the network will be trained on (in this example, 18 Hz, 20 Hz, A, B, and Noise). If you added random noise when creating the training images, Noise appears as one of the call types. Click Yes to proceed.







ImportantCall types are fixed once a network is trained



Because of MATLAB limitations, you cannot later add new call types to a network. If you want a network that detects additional call types in the future, you will need to train a new network from scratch with all of the call types included.





Training Settings
A series of dialogs then asks for the training settings. The first prompts you with the architecture you would like to select.

Base network
Choose the base network (architecture) to train from:

Tiny YOLO (pre-trained): the smallest and fastest to train. A good starting point for testing your other settings. This example uses Tiny YOLO.
CSP-DarkNet-53 (pre-trained): the largest and most complex architecture, with an extra detection head.
ResNet-50 (pre-trained): in between the two in size. It always uses an input size of 224 × 224 pixels.
ResNet-50 (blank): a ResNet-50 that has not been pre-trained. This option is still being evaluated.

See Available architectures for a comparison.


Image resolution
For Tiny YOLO and CSP-DarkNet-53, DeepAcoustics asks Would you like to reduce your image resolution b/c your GPU crashed the last time you tried this?

No - I believe in my GPU: keep the image resolution. Choose this if you have a reasonably powerful computer and GPU.
Yes - I want to edit: enter a smaller image size. Use this if training has previously crashed because your computer ran out of GPU memory.

These architectures require an image size that is a multiple of 32, so DeepAcoustics rounds the size automatically (for example, 300-pixel training images are used at 288 pixels). Choosing a size larger than the resolution you used to create the images does not add detail: the effective resolution stays at the resolution of your training images.


Customize or use defaults
DeepAcoustics asks whether you want to Customize your network options or use the Defaults. We recommend Customize in most cases. If you choose Defaults, DeepAcoustics uses 8 anchor boxes (9 for CSP-DarkNet-53), the SGDM solver, a learning rate of 0.01, a mini-batch size of 16, 30 epochs, and no validation data, and skips the rest of the settings below.


Anchor boxes
DeepAcoustics asks Do you already know how many anchor boxes you want to use?

Yes: enter the number of anchor boxes directly.
No: DeepAcoustics calculates the best anchor boxes for every count from 1 to 15 and plots the results so you can choose.

When you select No, here is what DeepAcoustics calculates:

For each number of anchors from 1 to 15, it groups the widths and heights of all the bounding boxes in your training images into that many clusters (using MATLAB’s estimateAnchorBoxes, a clustering method that groups boxes by how much they overlap). The center of each cluster becomes one anchor box shape.
For each count, it calculates the mean IoU: how well, on average, each of your annotated boxes overlaps with its closest-matching anchor shape. A mean IoU of 1 would mean every box matched an anchor exactly.
It plots Number of Anchors (x-axis) against Mean IoU (y-axis).


Choose the number where the curve starts to level off (the “elbow”). Beyond that point, adding more anchors improves the fit only slightly while increasing computation. In this example, the curve rises steeply up to about 6 anchors and then flattens, and 6 anchors has also worked well for us in the past, so we enter 6. We also recommend trying a few values and comparing the resulting networks.
If the number you enter does not suit the architecture, DeepAcoustics rounds it up: Tiny YOLO and ResNet-50 need an even number, and CSP-DarkNet-53 needs a multiple of three. See Anchor boxes for how anchor boxes work and how to choose the number.


Solver (optimizer)
The solver, or optimizer, is the algorithm that adjusts the network’s weights during training to reduce the loss (the error between the network’s predictions and your annotations). DeepAcoustics currently offers three:

sgdm (stochastic gradient descent with momentum): after each mini-batch, takes a step in the direction that reduces the loss, using the same step size (learning rate) for every weight. “Momentum” carries over part of the previous steps, which smooths out the path and helps it keep moving in a consistent direction. It is simple and reliable but can need more epochs to converge.
rmsprop (root mean square propagation): adjusts the step size separately for each weight, based on how large that weight’s recent updates have been. Weights with large or erratic updates take smaller steps, and weights with small, steady updates take larger ones. This often makes training more stable. RMSProp has worked well for us, and we typically use it with its default learning rate.
adam (adaptive moment estimation): combines the two ideas above: it uses momentum like SGDM and adjusts each weight’s step size like RMSProp. It often converges quickly and is a common default in deep learning.



Initial learning rate
The learning rate sets how large a step the solver takes each time it updates the weights. The suggested defaults are 0.01 for sgdm and 0.001 for rmsprop and adam. A rate that is too high can make training unstable (the loss jumps around or grows); a rate that is too low makes training very slow. If training runs into problems with your computing resources, try a lower rate. This is a setting worth experimenting with.


Mini-batch size
During training, the training images are shuffled and divided into small groups called mini-batches. The network processes one mini-batch, calculates the average loss across those images, and then updates its weights once. Each of these updates is one iteration, so the number of iterations in one epoch is roughly the number of training images divided by the mini-batch size.

Larger mini-batches give a more stable estimate of which direction to adjust the weights and need fewer updates per epoch, but they use more GPU memory.
Smaller mini-batches use less memory and make more frequent, noisier updates.

The default is 16, because larger architectures such as CSP-DarkNet-53 can run out of memory with bigger mini-batches. Smaller networks such as Tiny YOLO can usually handle larger mini-batches, such as 64 and above.


Maximum number of epochs
An epoch is one complete pass through all of the training images (see Key hyperparameters). The default maximum is 30. More epochs give the network more chances to learn, but training too long can lead to overfitting, where the network memorizes the training images instead of learning patterns that generalize to new data. Watch the training progress window (below) and stop early if the validation loss starts to rise.


Validation data
If you did not provide validation image tables, DeepAcoustics asks Would you like to use a proportion of your training data to validate (recommended to assess overfitting)?

Yes: set aside part of your training images for validation. These images are not used to train the network; instead, the network is checked against them during training to show how well it handles data it has not learned from. This is what lets you spot overfitting.
No: train on all of the images without validation (not recommended).


The dialog also warns that, because of MATLAB data type limitations, using validation data may stop the training images from being reshuffled between epochs, which could itself contribute to overfitting.
If you choose Yes, enter the proportion of your non-augmented training images to use for validation, as a decimal (the default is 0.1, or 10%). Augmented duplicates are never selected for validation. Studies have used validation proportions from about 10% up to 25%; we have found that about 0.2 (20%) works well, and that is what this example uses.

How the validation images are chosen
With a multiclass network, DeepAcoustics tries to make sure every call type is represented in the validation set:

It counts how many (non-augmented) training images contain each call type.
It multiplies the count for the rarest call type by your proportion. This becomes the number of validation images for every call type, so each call type gets roughly the same number of validation images.
Starting with the rarest call type, it randomly selects images containing each call type until that call type has its share. Because one image can contain several call types, images selected for one call type also count toward the others.

DeepAcoustics then shows a Check Proportions dialog with the percentage of each call type’s images that ended up in the validation set. The rarest call type will be close to the proportion you entered, and more common call types will be lower, because they all receive about the same number of validation images. In this example, with a proportion of 0.2, call type A (the rarest) is at 19.8%, and the more common call types are between 4.8% and 7.9%. Click Yes to proceed (clicking No cancels training).










Monitoring Training
Once the settings are confirmed, training begins and the Training Progress window opens.

TrainingLoss (blue line): the loss on the current mini-batch of training images, plotted at every iteration. It is usually very high at first and then drops quickly as the network starts to learn, before leveling off.
ValidationLoss (orange line): the loss on the validation images. It is calculated only every so often (every 50 iterations by default in MATLAB), so it appears as points joined by straight lines, which can look like a long straight line early in training.
Progress panel (right): shows the progress bar, start time, elapsed time, current epoch, iteration, and learning rate. The Export as Image button saves a picture of the plot.

How to read the curves is explained in Key hyperparameters. In short: if both losses fall together, the network is still learning; if both are low and stable, the fit is good; and if the validation loss starts to rise while the training loss keeps falling, the network is overfitting.






The MATLAB Command Window
While training runs, MATLAB also prints a progress table in the Command Window. It starts by listing the call types (object classes) the network is being trained on, then adds a row every 30 iterations, plus a row each time the validation loss is calculated:
Epoch   Iteration   TimeElapsed   LearnRate   TrainingLoss   ValidationLoss
  1         1        00:00:09       0.001        923.51          1380.1
  1        30        00:01:47       0.001        42.379
  2        50        00:02:51       0.001        26.871          31.749
  ...
  9       250        00:13:20       0.001        10.69           16.467
 10       300        00:15:56       0.001        8.3519          17.686
 10       310        00:16:27       0.001        8.2466          18.928

Epoch: which pass through the training images the network is on.
Iteration: how many weight updates (mini-batches) have been completed so far. In this example, 10 epochs took 310 iterations, or about 31 iterations per epoch.
TimeElapsed: the time since training started (hours:minutes:seconds).
LearnRate: the learning rate in use. It stays at the initial learning rate you entered throughout training.
TrainingLoss: the loss on the current mini-batch of training images.
ValidationLoss: the loss on the validation images. It is only filled in on the rows where it was calculated (every 50 iterations, and at the end of training); it is blank on the other rows. If you did not use validation data, this column does not appear.

When training is complete, MATLAB prints Detector training complete.
This table holds the same information as the Training Progress window, but as exact numbers, which makes it easier to see where the validation loss was lowest. In this example, the training loss keeps falling right to the end (from 923.51 to 8.2466), but the validation loss reaches its lowest value, 16.467, at iteration 250 (epoch 9) and then rises to 17.686 and 18.928. That rise while training loss keeps falling is an early sign of overfitting, and it suggests that about 9 epochs would have been enough for this dataset and these settings.


Early stopping
Early stopping means ending training before the maximum number of epochs, at the point where the network performs best on the validation data. If the validation loss stops improving or starts to rise while the training loss keeps falling, further training is likely to make the network worse at handling new data. To stop early, click the stop button (the round button to the right of the progress bar). The network is kept as it was when you stopped, so stop near the point where the validation loss was lowest. You can also use what you see to choose a smaller number of epochs the next time you train.


Saving the network






ImportantSave the trained network



When training finishes (or you stop it), DeepAcoustics opens a Save New Network dialog. You must save the network here, or the training will be lost. The network is saved as a .mat file, but the dialog does not suggest a file name, so give it a clear, descriptive name. For example, include the project or dataset, the architecture, the call types, and a version number, such as OOI_Multiclass_TinyYOLO_6anchors_v1.mat. Because training images, detections, and networks are all .mat files, a clear name makes it much easier to tell your networks apart later.


The network .mat file stores the trained detector together with the training options and the spectrogram settings used to create the training images (window size, overlap, NFFT, frequency limits, sampling rate, and image length), so DeepAcoustics knows how the network’s images were made when you use it to detect calls. Save it in your networks folder so it appears in the Neural Networks list in the main window.

title: Preparing Your Data
text:
Bounding Box Annotation for Object Detection
DeepAcoustics trains its detection networks on bounding box annotations. A bounding box annotation is more than a date and timestamp marking when a call occurred. It is a box drawn around the call itself on the spectrogram, and it records four values for each call:

Begin time: when the call starts.
End time: when the call ends.
Low frequency: the lower frequency limit of the call.
High frequency: the upper frequency limit of the call.

Each box is also given a label (for example, a call type or species) so the network can learn to tell different call types apart.






ImportantBox every call in the annotated audio



DeepAcoustics does not train on clipped snippets of individual calls. Instead, the full audio files are fed through the system, and the bounding boxes tell the network where the calls are within them. This means any call that is missed or left unboxed is treated as noise. During training, the network learns that the unboxed call is not a call of interest, which works against both detection and classification. Before training, make sure every call of interest in the annotated audio has been boxed and labeled.




Selecting the Correct Bandwidth
DeepAcoustics works best when your audio files are prepared to suit the signals you want to detect and classify. Some binary classification methods train on spectrograms, or on short audio clips converted to spectrograms, that are each framed around individual calls of varying bandwidth. DeepAcoustics works differently: it generates its images from the full duration of the audio files you provide. It does not currently decimate (downsample) the data or handle files of different bandwidths.
For this reason, two things are essential:

Use the same sampling rate throughout. The audio used to train, test, and deploy a network must all have the same sampling rate, and therefore the same bandwidth (half the sampling rate).
Choose a sampling rate suited to your calls. The sampling rate should capture the full frequency range of your calls without adding a lot of unneeded bandwidth. For example, a sampling rate of 48 or 96 kHz works best for delphinid calls, while a sampling rate of 400 Hz is better suited to low-frequency blue and fin whale calls.

If you are in need of a decimator for your audio dataset, visit our Bioacoustic Resources page for a free easy to use tool, EZ-AudioMate!


Annotating in Raven
DeepAcoustics can accept annotations from several sources, but the most common, and the format this guide focuses on, is the Raven selection table. Raven is a family of sound analysis software from the K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and is widely used for annotating marine and terrestrial sound recordings. In Raven, each annotated call is a “selection,” and a selection table is a tab-delimited text file listing every selection along with its time, frequency, and label information.
The tutorials in this guide highlight Raven Annotate, the newer component of Raven Workbench designed specifically for annotating calls within a dataset.

Saving a Raven Pro selection table from Raven Annotate
When you finish annotating in Raven Annotate, export your annotations by going to File > Export > Raven Pro Selection Table. If you are working in Raven, this is the format your annotations should be saved in for import into DeepAcoustics.
Note: DeepAcoustics can work with .wav audio files, or the compressed .flac version of audio files.




Raven Selection Table
DeepAcoustics reads Raven selection tables saved as tab-delimited .txt files (comma-separated .csv files are also accepted). Column names must match Raven’s standard names exactly, including the units in parentheses. Each call label must be in a column named Annotation.





The table below describes each column in a typical Raven Pro selection table and how DeepAcoustics uses it during import.








Column
Use in DeepAcoustics
Description




Selection
Not used
Raven’s ID number for each selection. Can be left in the table.


View
Not used
The Raven view the selection was made in (for example, “Spectrogram 1”). Can be left in the table.


Channel
Not used
The audio channel the selection was made on. DeepAcoustics always reads channel 1 of multichannel audio.


Begin Time (s)
Required unless File Offset (s) is present
Start time of the call, in seconds. Used when there is no File Offset (s) column.


End Time (s)
Required*
End time of the call, in seconds.


Low Freq (Hz)
Required
Lower frequency limit of the bounding box, in Hz.


High Freq (Hz)
Required
Upper frequency limit of the bounding box, in Hz.


Delta Time (s)
Required*
Duration of the call, in seconds.


Peak Freq (Hz)
Not used
Frequency with the most energy within the selection. Can be left in the table.


Begin File
Strongly recommended
Name of the audio file the call starts in. Lets DeepAcoustics match each call to the correct audio file, so one table can cover many files.


File Offset (s)
Required with Begin File
Start time of the call, in seconds, measured from the beginning of the file named in Begin File. When present, DeepAcoustics uses this instead of Begin Time (s).


Begin Date Time
Not used
Date and time the selection begins. Can be left in the table.


Annotation
Required
The call label (for example, call type or species). Used as the class name for training and detection. Calls with a blank annotation are imported as “Missing Annotation.”


Quality/Call Descriptor
Not used, but helpful for potential use later in classification/clustering
Optional notes column (for example, flagging a low-quality call). Can be left in the table.



*At least one of End Time (s) or Delta Time (s) must be present, so DeepAcoustics can calculate where each call ends.






TipWhy Begin File and File Offset (s) matter



If your selection table spans multiple audio files (for example, a day of 5-minute recordings), include the Begin File and File Offset (s) columns. Without them, DeepAcoustics tries to match each selection table to an audio file by filename, which only works when there is exactly one audio file per table and can cause unexpected behavior later on.
NOTE: Once you have a set of audio files annotated, eliminating specific files from a folder can be problematic on the Raven and DeepAcoustics end. It is best to annotate once your dataset (or subset) is selected to avoid additional data management steps.






DeepAcoustics Annotation File
If you prefer, you can create annotations directly in DeepAcoustics instead of using Raven.

Select your audio folder. Go to File > Select Audio Folder and choose the folder containing the audio you want to annotate.
Load the audio. In the Detect, Load, & Record section at the bottom of the window, select Load Audio:







Draw a bounding box. Under Annotation & Detection, select Draw (d), or press d on your keyboard, then draw a box around the call.
Choose a label. To change the annotation label assigned to the box, select Draw Label. A list of previously created labels appears, along with an option to create a new label. Select the label you want and press Enter to create the box:







Save your annotations. When you finish, select Save Session. Your annotations are saved in a DeepAcoustics detections file (.mat), which can be used for training and testing just like an imported Raven selection table.

title: DeepAcoustics Guide and Tutorial
text:
DeepAcoustics



About DeepAcoustics
DeepAcoustics is an open-access, MATLAB-based tool that was modified from a program called DeepSqueak (Coffey et al., 2019). Originally designed for use with ultrasonic calls from rats for neurological studies, our modification of the program has led to an independent version of the software that is optimized to detect calls in noisier, underwater environments. Additional modifications to the classification capabilities are incorporated in DeepAcoustics.
Modifications to DeepAcoustics allowed for a broadened scope that prioritizes underwater acoustic environments and species, while still accommodating in-air terrestrial counterparts. These enhancements extend the tool’s functionality, with key improvements including:

Access to wider bandwidth, including low frequencies that were not previously required for DeepSqueak.
Increased user interactivity in image creation, network training, and multiclass sound detection, ideal for analyzing overlapping call types across bandwidths.
Support for custom duration audio file sizes and integration with Raven selection tables, often used for marine call annotation.
Processing of large acoustic datasets, with the ability to extract date and time stamps directly from file names for streamlined data management.
Ongoing advancements in classification capabilities, ensuring the tool stays at the forefront of bioacoustic research.

These modifications build on the intuitive graphical user interface (GUI) originally developed by Coffey et al., ensuring DeepAcoustics remains accessible to users with varying levels of bioacoustic expertise. It provides a powerful, flexible deep learning tool that simplifies network training and deployment, empowering researchers to tackle both marine and terrestrial acoustic challenges efficiently.






NoteApplicable across species and frequency ranges



DeepAcoustics can be applied to a wide variety of terrestrial and marine species and across a broad range of frequency bandwidths. This guide and tutorial emphasize marine mammals because of our specialization in underwater acoustics, but the same workflow applies to other taxa and sound sources.


For access to this software, please visit the DeepAcoustics repository.



Software Requirements:
DeepAcoustics is developed in MATLAB and utilizes the streamlined integration of deep learning modules along with the YOLO (“You Only Look Once”) object detection model, specifically version 4. While this version is not as advanced as Python’s YOLO v9, it offers robust performance for bioacoustic applications. To run DeepAcoustics, the following are required:

MATLAB version R2023b or higher
Deep Learning Toolbox
Computer Vision Toolbox
Signal Processing Toolbox
Parallel Computing Toolbox (for GPU support)
Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox

These requirements ensure optimal performance and efficient handling of deep learning tasks within the software.



GPU Requirements:
A GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) is a specialized hardware component designed to handle complex mathematical calculations, especially those related to graphics rendering and parallel processing tasks. While GPUs were originally developed for rendering images and videos in gaming and 3D applications, their architecture has made them highly effective for tasks that involve large-scale matrix and vector operations, which are common in deep learning.
Deep learning tasks, such as training neural networks, require the processing of vast amounts of data and the performance of many computations simultaneously. These tasks involve operations like multiplying large matrices (weights and inputs), calculating gradients, and updating model parameters across multiple layers of the network. CPUs (Central Processing Units) can handle these tasks but are optimized for sequential processing, meaning they are generally slower when performing the parallelized operations deep learning demands. GPUs, on the other hand, are designed to process thousands of operations in parallel, making them much faster for deep learning tasks. This capability is essential when working with large datasets and complex models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or object detection models like YOLO, where speed and efficiency are crucial. By using GPUs, deep learning models can be trained faster and more efficiently, significantly reducing the time needed for both training and inference, particularly when working with large-scale or real-time applications.
A modern GPU with CUDA support is required for training networks in DeepAcoustics, but is not required for using a trained network model to detect target calls in audio using DeepAcoustics.



Getting Started
This documentation takes users through the features of DeepAcoustics, and then includes a tutorial that users can use for further exploration of this deep learning GUI. Please begin by downloading DeepAcoustics from the GitHub repository below. Then open MATLAB, set the path to the folder you downloaded the software to, and use the word “DeepAcoustics” to call the tool. We recommend using GitHub Desktop to streamline the incorporation of updates to the software.
Access DeepAcoustics








How to Get Help

Software Issues
If you encounter any issues or have questions about DeepAcoustics, please visit the DeepAcoustics Software Issues section. To help us resolve problems efficiently, include the following details when reporting an issue:

MATLAB version you’re using
Platform and OS version (e.g., Windows 11, macOS Ventura)
Steps or code that triggered the issue
What happened vs. what you expected
Any error messages or unusual behavior
Apply the appropriate description in the title (e.g., “Training Bug”)



Discussions
For general inquiries, ideas, or feedback that don’t fit into an issue report, use the Discussions section. This space is ideal for:

Sharing ideas or suggestions for new features
Discussing best practices for using the software effectively
Engaging with other users to ask questions or share insights

Both sections are monitored to ensure you receive timely support and can connect with the broader DeepAcoustics community.
