title: Creating Training Images
text:
Before DeepAcoustics can train a detection network, it converts your annotated audio into a set of spectrogram images, each paired with the bounding boxes of the calls it contains. This page walks through creating those training images and explains each of the image settings.
The example on this page uses five training annotation (detections) files containing blue whale A and B calls and fin whale 18 Hz and 20 Hz calls, recorded on Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI) hydrophones off Newport, Oregon. These files are part of a Dryad repository from a recent multiclass baleen whale effort, available here: Annotated training and evaluation data and DeepAcoustics-derived networks for multi-class baleen whale calls (doi: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.x0k6djj2d)


Creating the Images

Open the tool. Go to Tools > Network Training > Create Detection Network Training Images.
Select the detection files. Choose one or more detections files to build the training images from, then click Open. In this example, all five files are selected. Keeping your annotations in separate detections files (for example, by site, deployment, or call type) makes it easy to train on different combinations of files later.
Choose the call types. As each file loads, DeepAcoustics asks which call types to include. Each file lists the call types annotated in it, so the options can differ from file to file. This lets you annotate everything in your data once and then train a network for only certain species or call types. In this example, all call types are selected in every file.
Set the training image settings. The Settings for Training Images dialog opens. The settings are described in detail below. Click OK when you are done.

Select the output folder. Choose the folder where the training images will be saved. If you turned on Manually Select Validation Data, DeepAcoustics then asks for the validation detections files and a separate folder for the validation images (see below).
Let the images generate. DeepAcoustics creates the spectrogram images, and you will see them start to appear in your output folder. Augmented duplicates, if any, are saved in an ImgAug subfolder.
Review the summary and save the image table. When finished, DeepAcoustics shows a summary of the calls and noise included (see Understanding the summary) and asks where to save the image table. By default, it is named after the first detections file, followed by &More if you selected more than one file, and _Images.mat. This .mat file lists every training image and the bounding boxes in it, along with the spectrogram settings used, and it is what you select when training the network.








WarningChoose the image table location carefully



The image table stores the full path to each training image. If you move or rename the image folder after creating the table, DeepAcoustics will not be able to find the images. Decide where the images and table will live before you create them. (A fix for this is in progress.)





Training Image Settings
The Settings for Training Images dialog controls how your audio is turned into images. These settings matter a great deal for network performance, so it is worth taking time to choose them.

Annotation metadata
At the top of the dialog, DeepAcoustics summarizes the annotations you selected, to help you choose the settings below:

Min Dur (s) and Max Dur (s): the shortest and longest annotated call, in seconds.
Median Dur (s): the median call duration.
90% Quant Dur (s): the duration that 90% of your calls are shorter than. This is a useful guide for image length because it ignores the few very longest calls.
Min Freq (Hz) and Max Freq (Hz): the lowest and highest upper frequency limit among your annotated boxes. Use Max Freq (Hz) to check that your High Frequency Cutoff (Hz) is high enough to include your calls.
Min SR (Hz) and Max SR (Hz): the lowest and highest sampling rate among your audio files. These should be the same. If your files have different sampling rates, DeepAcoustics warns you and uses the lowest one.



Spectrogram settings
These settings work the same way as the spectrogram settings described under Display Settings, but here they control the training images rather than the display. Make sure the window size and NFFT suit the call types you are training on.

Units of Spectrogram Parameters: whether Window Size and NFFT are entered as a number of Samples or as a duration in Seconds.

When using Samples, DeepAcoustics treats the sample counts as if the audio were sampled at twice the High Frequency Cutoff (Hz) (the “effective Nyquist” noted in red in the dialog). If you change the High Frequency Cutoff, the sample counts are updated automatically so the window keeps the same duration in seconds.

Low Frequency Cutoff (Hz) and High Frequency Cutoff (Hz): the frequency range included in the training images. The High Frequency Cutoff defaults to half the sampling rate and must not be set above the bandwidth available in your audio. Any part of a call that falls outside this range is excluded from training, and DeepAcoustics warns you if this happens.
Window Size: the length of each chunk of audio analyzed for one column of the spectrogram. Longer windows give finer frequency resolution but blur timing; shorter windows show timing more sharply but blur frequency.
Overlap (%): how much each window overlaps the next. It must be less than 95%.
NFFT: the number of points in the Fourier transform of each window, which sets the spacing between frequency bins. It is usually set equal to the window size.



Image settings

Image Length (s): the duration of audio shown in each training image. By default, it is set to twice the 90% quantile duration (rounded), unless Optimize is on.
Optimize: when this button is pressed in (highlighted), DeepAcoustics calculates the image length automatically so that each pixel across the image represents exactly one time step of the spectrogram. The image length then updates on its own whenever you change the NFFT, Overlap (%), or Image Resolution (pixels), and the Image Length field cannot be edited. Press it again to turn it off and enter an image length yourself.
Image Resolution (pixels): the width and height of each training image, in pixels. Images are always square, and the default is 300 × 300. Larger images can show more detail, but they take longer to train and use more memory, and you will eventually run into the limits of your computer.
# of Augmented Duplicates: how many extra, slightly altered copies of each training image to create. Each duplicate randomly varies the image contrast and the FFT size (up to two powers of two smaller or larger than your setting), which gives the network more varied examples. This can help when you have a small number of training annotations. The default is 0 (no duplicates).



Toggles

Randomly Add Noise: when set to Yes, DeepAcoustics adds “Noise” boxes to unannotated parts of your audio before creating the images. It aims for roughly as many noise boxes as calls, with sizes based on the range of your call box sizes and within your frequency limits. This gives the network examples of what is not a call. We recommend Yes, unless noise has already been annotated in your files (if a file already contains Noise, DeepAcoustics skips it).
Manually Select Validation Data: controls how validation data are chosen. Validation data are held back from training and used to check how well the network is learning (and whether it is overfitting) as training progresses.

No: all of your selected files are used for training images, and a percentage of them is automatically set aside for validation during training. This is the simplest option and was the only option in earlier versions of DeepAcoustics.
Yes: after you click OK, you choose separate detections files to use only for validation, plus a separate output folder for the validation images, which must be different from the training image folder. DeepAcoustics creates a second image table (ending in _ValImages.mat). This gives you more control over exactly which calls and audio files are used for validation, which can ultimately produce a more robust network.

In this example, Manually Select Validation Data is set to No because all of the annotations are in one folder, and with multiclass data it is harder to set aside a healthy sample of every call type for both training and validation.







WarningRandomly adding noise changes your detections files



When Randomly Add Noise is set to Yes, the new noise boxes are written into your existing detections files. Keep a backup copy of your detections files if you want to preserve the originals.






Choosing Image Length and Resolution

Why image length matters
DeepAcoustics is an object detection tool, so the training images should not be cropped tightly around each call. The network needs to see the call in context, including the background noise around it, so it can learn what is and is not a call. A longer image length captures more representative noise around each bounding box, and an image can contain several annotations. An image length that is too short is a problem because it does not capture enough of that surrounding noise.
As a rule of thumb, an image length of about 2 to 3 times the duration of your longest typical call includes a good amount of noise. If a call is longer than the image length, it is split across images, and DeepAcoustics reports how many calls were split in the summary.


How Optimize calculates image length
Each column of pixels in a training image should ideally represent one time step (hop) of the spectrogram. Optimize uses this to calculate the image length:

Time step (hop) in seconds = NFFT in seconds × (1 − Overlap ÷ 100)
Optimized image length = time step × Image Resolution (pixels)

For the example dataset shown in the dialog (a 400 Hz sampling rate with a High Frequency Cutoff of 200 Hz, an NFFT of 512 samples, 90% overlap, and an image resolution of 300 pixels):

NFFT in seconds = 512 ÷ 400 Hz = 1.28 s
Time step = 1.28 s × 0.1 = 0.128 s
Optimized image length = 0.128 s × 300 pixels = 38.4 s

As another example, with a 32,000 Hz sampling rate, an NFFT of 1024 samples, 90% overlap, and 288 pixels, the time step is 1024 ÷ 32,000 × 0.1 = 0.0032 s, giving an optimized image length of about 0.92 s.

If the image is longer than this, neighboring time steps are squeezed together to fit the available pixels, so some time resolution is lost.
If the image is shorter than this, several pixels are used to show the same time step, which is an inefficient use of the image.
Doubling the NFFT (for example, from 1024 to 2048) doubles the optimized image length, because each time step becomes twice as long. It also increases the frequency detail, which the available pixels may not be able to show in full.

When you click OK, DeepAcoustics also checks your settings and warns you if the image resolution is smaller than the number of frequency bins in your chosen bandwidth, or smaller than the number of time steps in your image length. In either case, some detail will be lost when the spectrogram is resized to fit the image.






NoteBalancing image length against calls being split



If your longest calls are much longer than the optimized image length, you have a trade-off: keep the optimized length and accept that some calls are split across images, or use a longer image length and accept lower time resolution. There is no single right answer, and the best way to find out which works better for your calls is to try both and compare the resulting networks.




Image resolution and the network input size
The image resolution sets how many pixels each training image has, not how much time or frequency it shows. Every training image covers exactly the same duration and bandwidth.
When you train, the images are resized to the network’s input size. This is a change in resolution, not a “zoom” into part of the image: the whole image is kept and simply shown with more or fewer pixels.

TinyYOLO requires an input size that is a multiple of 32, so a 300-pixel image is rounded to 288 pixels.
CSP-DarkNet-53 asks you for an input size, because 288 pixels may be too large for your GPU.
ResNet-50 uses a fixed input size of 224 × 224.





Understanding the Summary
When the images have been created, DeepAcoustics displays a summary box like this one, from the example dataset:
Final Call Information:
# Total Calls in Det Files: 4168
# Whole Calls in Images File: 3734
# Split Calls in Images File: 434
# Total Call Pieces in Images File: 4580
# Noise in Images File: 2287
# Total Calls in Det Files (Val): 0
# Whole Calls in Images File (Val): 0
# Split Calls in Images File (Val): 0
# Total Call Pieces in Images File (Val): 0
# Noise in Images File (Val): 0

# Total Calls in Det Files: the number of accepted calls (not including noise) in the detections files you selected. Rejected calls are not used. The example has 4,168 calls.
# Whole Calls in Images File: calls that fit entirely within a single image (3,734 in the example).
# Split Calls in Images File: calls that were longer than the image length, or fell across an image boundary, and had to be split across images (434 in the example). Whole calls plus split calls always add up to the total number of calls (3,734 + 434 = 4,168).
# Total Call Pieces in Images File: the total number of call boxes across all images, counting each piece of a split call separately. In the example, the 434 split calls became 846 pieces, so the images contain 3,734 + 846 = 4,580 call boxes.
# Noise in Images File: the number of noise boxes included (2,287 in the example). This count currently also includes the noise in augmented duplicates.
(Val) counts: the same counts for the validation images. These are only filled in if you set Manually Select Validation Data to Yes. In the example, they are all 0 because no separate validation files were selected; instead, a portion of the training images is randomly set aside for validation when the network is trained.







TipChecking for split calls



A large number of split calls means many calls are longer than your image length. In the example, about 10% of calls were split, which reflects the long blue whale calls relative to the image length. If many of your calls are being split, consider a longer image length (see Choosing Image Length and Resolution).


The number of calls is not the same as the number of images. A single image can contain several calls, and each noise box gets its own image, so the two counts will usually differ. After you save the image table, the MATLAB Command Window reports the total number of images created (for example, “Created 2751 Training Images”). This is the number of images in the image table, including augmented duplicates, and should match the number of image files in your output folder and its ImgAug subfolder.

title: Network Deployment
text:
Once you have a network that performs well on your test data (see Performance Testing), you can use it to detect calls in new audio. This page covers running the network on your audio, how DeepAcoustics turns the network’s raw output into detection boxes, adding the date and time to each detection, and exporting the detections to a Raven selection table.


Detecting Calls

Before you start

Select the audio folder. Go to File > Select Audio Folder and choose the folder containing the audio you want to run the network on.
Select the network folder. Go to File > Select Network Folder and choose the folder containing your trained network(s). If no network folder is selected, DeepAcoustics shows a No Network Selected error and you cannot run detection.



Running detection

Start detection. In the Detect, Load, & Record section, select Detect Calls. If you have unsaved changes to a detections file that is already loaded, DeepAcoustics first asks whether you want to save them.
Select the audio files. Select all of the audio files you want to analyze. You can select as many files as you like, so you can run the network on any amount of data at once.
Select the network. A list shows every network in your network folder. Select the network you want to use.
Select the output folder. Choose the folder where the detections file will be saved.
Enter the settings for running the network. The Settings for Running dialog (titled with the network’s name) has three settings, described on the Performance Testing page:

Total Analysis Length (Seconds; 0 = Full Duration): use 0 to analyze each audio file in full.
Score Threshold (0-1): the minimum confidence score a detection needs to be kept. You can use the precision-recall results from performance testing to choose a value; 0 keeps every detection.
Append Date to FileName (1 = yes): enter 1 to add the date and time of the run to the detections file name.

The frequency limits are not entered here: they are taken from the network, so the audio is processed with the same settings that were used to create the network’s training images. Click OK to start.



Monitoring progress
While the network runs, a progress bar shows:

Detection Speed: how many times faster than real time the audio is being processed. For example, 2000x means 2000 seconds of audio are processed every second. Tiny YOLO can reach about 2000x on long audio files. Larger architectures such as CSP-DarkNet-53 and ResNet-50 run more slowly, and the bandwidth (frequency range) of the network may also affect the speed. Your computing resources will also impact this speed.

Call Fragments Found: the number of raw detections (fragments) found so far in the current file, before they are merged into calls (see below).
File: which audio file is being processed, out of the total number selected.

The MATLAB Command Window also shows progress for each audio file:

Freq cut-offs (given spec settings) set to X Hz and Y Hz: the frequency range of the spectrograms the network is run on.
N Calls found in: [audio file]: the number of calls in that file after merging. Files with no detections are listed as No Calls found in: [audio file].
Warnings may appear if the audio has more than one channel (the channels are averaged) or if its sampling rate does not match the network (the audio is resampled or clipped to match the network’s frequency range).




Saving the detections
When all files are processed, DeepAcoustics saves the detections automatically. There is no save dialog. The detections file is saved in the output folder you selected, and its name is built from the name of the first audio file, the number of audio files, and _Detections.mat:
[first audio file]_[N]AudFiles_Detections.mat
If you entered 1 for Append Date to FileName, the date and time of the run is added before _Detections.mat. The file is only saved if at least one call was found.
You can then load the detections file with Load Detections to review the detections (see Annotation Review).




How Call Fragments Are Merged
The network does not see a whole audio file at once. DeepAcoustics breaks each file into short pieces, runs the network on each piece, and then merges the results into calls. This is why the progress bar counts call fragments while the Command Window reports calls.

Step 1: running the network on overlapping windows

Windows the length of a training image. Each audio file is split into windows the same length as the network’s training images (the image length stored in the network). Each window starts 80% of an image length after the previous one, so neighboring windows overlap by 20% of an image length. The overlap means a call that falls on the edge of one window also appears in the next.
One spectrogram per window. Each window is turned into a spectrogram using the network’s spectrogram settings and frequency limits, and processed in the same way as the training images.
Raw detections. The network detects calls in each spectrogram, keeping only the strongest of any boxes that overlap heavily within that window. Each detection has a box, a call type, and a confidence score. These raw detections are the call fragments.

A call can produce more than one fragment. For example, a call that crosses the boundary between two windows may be detected partly in one window and partly in the next, and a long call may be boxed in pieces.


Step 2: merging fragments into calls
After the whole file has been processed, DeepAcoustics merges the fragments:

Sort by time. All fragments in the file are sorted by start time.
Compare in time only. Fragments are compared using their start and end times only; their frequencies are ignored for this step. Any overlap in time counts, however small.
Same call type only. Fragments are only merged if they have the same call type. Overlapping fragments of different call types stay separate.
Chains are merged together. If fragment 1 overlaps fragment 2, and fragment 2 overlaps fragment 3, all three are merged into one call, even if fragments 1 and 3 do not overlap each other.
The merged box covers every fragment. Each merged call starts at the earliest start time and ends at the latest end time of its fragments, and spans from the lowest to the highest frequency of its fragments.
The score is the average. The merged call’s confidence score is the mean of its fragments’ scores, and it takes the call type of its fragments.
Apply the score threshold. Only merged calls with a score above the Score Threshold you entered are kept. Because the threshold is applied after merging, it is the average score of the fragments that counts, not the score of any single fragment.
Keep boxes inside the audio. Boxes are trimmed so they do not extend past the start or end of the audio file or outside its frequency range.

Every detection is saved as accepted, with no date or time yet.






NoteCalls of the same type that overlap in time are merged



Because fragments are compared in time only, two separate calls of the same type that overlap in time are merged into one detection, even if they are at different frequencies. For example, two overlapping calls of the same type from different animals would appear as a single box covering both. Calls of different types are never merged.






Adding the Date and Time
The detections file stores each call’s start time in seconds from the start of its audio file. Add Date/Time adds the actual date and time of each call, based on the date and time in the audio file names.

Open the tool. Go to Tools > File Management > Add Date/Time.
Read the overwrite warning. DeepAcoustics warns that the detections files you choose will be updated and overwritten. If you are unsure, make a backup copy of the detections file first. Click Yes to continue.
Select the detections file(s). Select the detections file. You can select more than one if they are in the same folder.

For each call, DeepAcoustics reads the start date and time of its audio file from the file name and adds the call’s start time within the file. The result is saved in the StTime column of the detections, in the format yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS (to the millisecond). Calls that already have a date and time are not changed.

Supported file name formats
DeepAcoustics looks for the date and time in the audio file names in these formats, where .* means any characters in between:

YYYYMMDD.*HHMMSS: a four-digit year, for example 20170108_133500.
YYMMDD.*HHMMSS: a two-digit year, for example HYDBBA103OOI_170108-133500.
YYMMDD.*HHMM: a two-digit year without seconds (seconds are set to 0).
YYYY-MM-DD.HH-MM-SS or YYYY_MM_DD.HH_MM_SS: with dashes or underscores, for example 2017-01-08T13-35-00.
SanctSound file names.

Four-digit years must start with 20, so dates must be in the year 2000 or later. DeepAcoustics also checks that the date and time are valid (for example, a month from 1 to 12 and an hour from 0 to 23).


Checking the date and time
At the moment, DeepAcoustics does not show a confirmation when the date and time have been added. If the file names could not be read, a warning appears in the MATLAB Command Window (Date/time format not recognizable - please use YYMMDD.*HHMMSS), and the calls are left without a date and time.
To check that the date and time were added:

Drag the detections file into the MATLAB Command Window (or double-click it in the MATLAB Current Folder panel) to load it into the workspace.
In the Workspace panel, double-click the Calls table.

Scroll to the right to the StTime column and check that it contains the date and time of each call.






Exporting to a Raven Selection Table
You can export the detections to a Raven selection table (.txt) to view them in Raven or use them in other software.

Load the detections. Export to Raven exports the detections file that is currently loaded, so first load it with Load Detections (see Importing Data).
Open the export. Go to File > Import/Export > Export to Raven.
Choose the type of selection table. DeepAcoustics asks whether to save a Sound Selection Table or a Selection Table. We recommend Selection Table. Note that Sound Selection Table is highlighted as the default in the dialog, so make sure to select Selection Table.
Save the table. Choose where to save the table. The default name is the detections file name followed by _Raven.txt.


Selection Table vs. Sound Selection Table

Selection Table: the original (legacy) Raven format. Begin and end times are counted continuously across all of the audio files in the detections file, as if they were one long recording. This matches how Raven displays a set of audio files opened together, so open all of the audio files in Raven and then open the table.
Sound Selection Table: begin and end times are counted from the start of each call’s own audio file, and the table lists the audio file for each call, so Raven can open the audio from the table. Raven will not load audio files that have no detections when you open a Sound Selection Table.




What is exported
Only accepted calls are exported. Rejected calls are left out, so the selection numbers may skip where calls were rejected. The table has these columns:

Selection: the call’s number in the detections file.
View and Channel: set to Spectrogram 1 and channel 1.
TimeStamp: the call’s date and time (StTime), if it has been added with Add Date/Time.
Begin Time (s) and End Time (s): the call’s start and end times, counted as described above for the type of table.
Low Freq (Hz) and High Freq (Hz): the call’s lowest and highest frequencies.
Delta Time (s) and Delta Freq (Hz): the call’s duration and bandwidth.
Avg Power Density (dB FS): not calculated by DeepAcoustics; filled with 1 as a placeholder.
Annotation: the call type.
Begin Path and Begin File: the full path and the file name of the call’s audio file.
File Offset: the call’s start time within its own audio file, in seconds.

title: Classification
text:
Clustering groups calls by how similar they are, without needing labels. This is useful for exploring a call repertoire: how many distinct call types there are, what they look like, and which calls are hard to place. DeepAcoustics offers two kinds of clustering:

Contour clustering: groups tonal calls, such as whistles, by the shape of their traced frequency contour. This is available now and is described on this page. A step-by-step walkthrough is coming soon.
Whole-image clustering with VAE and VGG: groups calls by the content of their whole spectrogram image, which suits complex calls that cannot be described by a single contour. This is new and still under development.



Key Terms
Unsupervised clustering: grouping data without any labels. The algorithm decides which calls belong together based only on how similar they are.
k-means clustering: the clustering method DeepAcoustics uses. You choose (or DeepAcoustics searches for) a number of clusters, k. Each cluster has a center, or centroid, and each call is assigned to the cluster whose centroid it is closest to. The centroids are adjusted until the assignments stop changing.
Replicates: the number of times k-means is run, each time from different starting centroids. The best of the runs is kept. More replicates give more reliable clusters but take longer.
Contour: the line traced along the peak frequency of a call over time.



Contour Clustering
Contour clustering describes each call by the shape of its contour and then groups calls with similar shapes using k-means.

Before you start

Review your detections. Only accepted calls are clustered, and calls labeled Noise are left out, so review your detections first (see Annotation Review).
Check the contours. Contour clustering is only as good as the traced contours. Background noise, overlapping calls, and harmonics can pull the trace off the call. The contour of the selected call is shown in the Contour panel on the left of the main window, and you can remove or add points that do not fit the call with the contour editing tool before clustering.




The contour of the selected call (circled) is shown on the left of the main window.




Running contour clustering

Open the tool. Go to Tools > Call Classification > Unsupervised Clustering.
Choose the clustering method. Select Contour Parameters (recommended).
Choose whether to use a saved model. Select No to build a new clustering model, or Yes to apply a model you saved earlier to new data.
Select the detections file(s). You can select more than one.
Set the contour parameters and choose how many clusters to use (see below).



Contour parameters
Each contour is resampled to a set number of evenly spaced points, and several features are measured at those points. Each feature has a weight, which sets how much it counts when calls are compared. A weight of 0 leaves that feature out.

Number of Contour Pts: the number of points each contour is resampled to (default 20). More points capture more detail; complex shapes, such as sine waves with several turns, may need more points (we have used 50) to be told apart.
Relative Frequency Weight: the frequency at each point relative to the start of the call, so all contours start at zero. This compares shapes regardless of the call’s absolute frequency (default weight 10).
Slope Weight: how quickly the frequency is rising or falling at each point (default weight 5).
Concavity Weight: how the slope is changing at each point, which picks out curves and turns in the contour (default weight 4).
Other parameters: absolute frequency, duration, number of inflection points (where the contour changes from curving up to curving down), and others. These are off (weight 0) by default.



Choosing the number of clusters
DeepAcoustics then asks how to choose the number of clusters:

Elbow Optimized: tries every number of clusters up to a maximum and plots the error (how far calls are from their cluster centers) against the number of clusters. It picks the “elbow”, where adding more clusters stops reducing the error much.
Elbow w/ Min Clust Size: as above, but if any cluster has fewer calls than the minimum cluster size, it reduces the number of clusters until every cluster is large enough. A minimum of 2 removes clusters made of a single call (singletons).
User Defined: you enter the number of clusters.
User Defined w/ Min Clust Size: you enter a starting number of clusters, and DeepAcoustics reduces it until every cluster meets the minimum size.
Silhouette Batch: runs the clustering for a range of cluster numbers and plots silhouette values (see below) for each, so you can compare them.




Example elbow plot. The red point marks the elbow, here at 11 clusters.






Clustering Results
When clustering finishes, DeepAcoustics shows several figures to help you judge the clusters.

t-SNE plot
t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding): a way of drawing high-dimensional data in two dimensions. Calls that are similar are placed close together, and calls that are different are placed further apart. Each point is a call, colored and shaped by its cluster. Tight, well-separated groups suggest distinct call types; overlapping groups suggest call types that are hard to separate. The distances between groups on a t-SNE plot are only a rough guide, so use it to explore rather than to measure.



Example t-SNE plot from contour clustering of bottlenose dolphin whistles, with 44 clusters.




Silhouette plot
Silhouette value: a measure, from -1 to 1, of how well each call fits its own cluster compared with the next closest cluster.

Close to 1: the call fits its cluster well and is far from other clusters.
Around 0: the call is on the border between two clusters.
Below 0: the call may fit better in another cluster.

The silhouette plot shows a bar for each call, grouped by cluster. The red dashed line is the overall mean silhouette value and the green dotted line is the median. The title also lists summary values, such as the proportion of calls at or below 0 and the number of singletons. Clusters with mostly long bars are well defined; clusters with short or negative bars contain calls that resist categorization.



Example silhouette plot for the same 44 clusters.




Other figures

Centroid Contours with Max and Min Call Variation: the average contour shape of each cluster, with the range of its calls (shown when Relative Frequency is used).
Closest call to each cluster center: the spectrogram of the most representative call in each cluster.



Reviewing and saving clusters
The Clustering Dialog then lets you page through the calls in each cluster, look at their spectrograms, and name the clusters. You can save the clustering model, to apply it to new data later, and the extracted contours with each call’s cluster assignment.



The Clustering Dialog, showing the calls in one cluster.




Other tools in the Call Classification menu

View Clusters: open the Clustering Dialog for detections files you have already clustered, review or rename the clusters, and update the files with the changes.
Create t-SNE / UMAP Embedding: create a t-SNE plot of your calls on its own, based on their contour shape, frequency, and duration (or on VAE embeddings). The UMAP option is not currently active.
Syntax Analysis: explore the order in which call types occur within bouts of calling.







NoteWhat we are working on: synthetic whistles



We are developing a hybrid approach that adds a set of synthetic whistles with known shapes (upsweeps, downsweeps, constant frequency, convex and concave shapes) to the natural whistles before clustering. Because the synthetic whistles have a known answer, they help guide the clusters and check how well the clustering is working.






Whole-Image Clustering: VAE and VGG






WarningUnder development



Whole-image clustering with VAE and VGG is new and still under development. This section gives an overview of what is coming. Check back later for updates and step-by-step instructions.


Contour clustering works well for tonal calls with one clear contour, such as whistles. Many calls, such as humpback whale social calls, are pulsed, harmonic, or complex and cannot be described by a single contour. Whole-image clustering uses the entire spectrogram image of each call instead.

Key terms
Dimensionality reduction: summarizing a high-resolution spectrogram image, made up of thousands of pixel values, into a much smaller set of numbers that captures its key features.
Latent space: the compressed space in which a model represents the features of each image.
Embedding: the set of numbers (a vector) that represents one call in the latent space. You can think of it as the call’s “fingerprint”. Calls with similar embeddings are clustered together with k-means.



How the two methods represent a call in the latent space.




Variational autoencoder (VAE)
A variational autoencoder is a generative model with two parts. The encoder compresses each spectrogram into the latent space, and the decoder tries to rebuild the spectrogram from it. Rather than a single point, the encoder describes each call as a region in the latent space (a mean and a spread), which is why it is called probabilistic. In DeepAcoustics, the VAE is trained on your call spectrograms (resized to 128 × 128 pixels) with no pre-training, and the mean of each call’s encoding is used for k-means clustering. It appears as Auto Encoder + Contour in the clustering method dialog.


Visual Geometry Group network (VGG)
VGG-16 is a convolutional neural network with 13 convolutional layers and 3 fully connected layers. Here it is used as a feature extractor: each spectrogram (224 × 224 pixels) is passed through the network, which produces one fixed embedding for each call that is the same every time. These embeddings are then clustered.


What we are testing

Fitting calls to one image size: calls differ in duration and bandwidth, but these networks need every image to be the same size. We are testing different ways to do this, such as resizing the call’s spectrogram or placing it on a background of noise.
Comparing the methods: in our tests on humpback whale calls, VGG produced more visually cohesive clusters than the standard VAE model, which needs further optimization and higher resolution.
Next steps: pre-trained networks and more customization.

title: Annotation Review
text:
Once your annotations or detections are in a DeepAcoustics detections file, you can review them to correct labels, accept or reject calls, and weed out false positives. DeepAcoustics offers two ways to do this: reviewing calls one at a time in the main window, or batch reviewing many calls at once with the Call Review tool. The examples on this page use a multiclass detections file containing both blue whale (A and B) and fin whale (18 Hz and 20 Hz) calls.


Reviewing Calls in the Main Window

Loading a multiclass detections file

Load the detections. Go to File > Load Detections and select your detections file. Because this file contains more than one call type, a dialog lists the available call types and asks which ones to load.
Select all call types. In most cases, click Select all and then OK. You can still limit what is displayed afterward with Filter Display (see below), without risking the loss of any calls when you save.

Choose a starting audio file. Select the first audio file in the dataset (or wherever you want to begin) and click OK.







ImportantLoading only some call types affects what is saved



If you load only some of the call types and then save the session under the same file name, DeepAcoustics overwrites the original file and the call types you did not load are discarded. Loading all call types and using Filter Display avoids this.
You can also use this behavior on purpose. For example, to create a file containing only A calls, load only the A calls and then save the session under a new file name. The new file contains only A calls, and the original file is left unchanged.




Filtering the display
In the Detect, Load, & Record section, select Filter Display to choose which call types are shown. For example, select only A and B to display just the blue whale calls in the file. The other call types stay in the file; they are only hidden from view. To show everything again, select Filter Display and choose all call types. Filtering is a convenient way to review a multiclass file one call type at a time.


Reviewing individual calls
The main window is set up for reviewing calls one at a time, for example to work through a network’s detections and sort true detections from false positives. The currently selected call is shown with a bolder, highlighted box in the spectrogram. The controls in the Annotation & Detection section all act on that call, and each has a keyboard shortcut so you can move quickly:

Accept Call (a): accepts the selected call and moves straight to the next one. To review a set of detections quickly, press a for each call that is correct.
Reject Call (r): rejects the selected call, relabels it as Noise, and moves to the next one. Use it for false positives as you work through the file.
Play Call (p): plays the audio inside the selected call’s box, at the rate set by Change Playback Rate in the File menu.
Draw (d): draws a new box, for example to add a call the network missed (see Preparing Your Data).
Draw Label: sets the label used for new boxes and for relabeling.
Re-Label (w): changes the label of the selected call to the label shown next to Draw Label. Select Draw Label first to choose the correct label.








WarningAccepting a call can also change its label



If a call has not already been accepted, Accept Call (a) also changes its label to the one currently shown next to Draw Label. Before accepting calls, make sure Draw Label is set to the correct call type, or calls may be relabeled without you noticing.


When you finish, select Save Session. If you made changes and want to keep the original file intact, save under a new file name.




Batch Review with Call Review
The Call Review tool displays many calls at once as a grid of small spectrograms, so you can scan through a detections file quickly. It is especially useful for finding and removing false positives from a network’s detections.

Opening Call Review

Open the tool. Go to Tools > Call Review.
Select the detections file. Choose the detections .mat file you want to review. Call Review opens the file directly, so it does not need to be loaded in the main window first.
Choose the call types to review. In the list on the left, select the call type(s) you want to see and click Apply Selection. Hold Ctrl to select more than one call type.








Call Review settings

# of Calls to Display: how many calls are shown on each page of the grid (for example, 20).
Time Pad (sec): extra time added before and after each call, in seconds, so you can see the call in context (for example, 1 second on either side).
Freq Pad (Hz): extra frequency range added above and below each call, in Hz (for example, 20 Hz), to frame the call better.
Call #: the number of the first call shown. Type a number to jump to that call. The total number of calls of the selected type(s) is shown beside it.
Prev and Next: move back or forward one page of calls.

Each spectrogram in the grid is titled with its position on the page, followed by the call’s ID number and its current label in parentheses.

Select calls. Click a spectrogram to select it; selected calls appear faded. Click it again to deselect it. You can select as many calls as you like, or use Select/De-select All to select or clear every call on the page.
Change the label of selected calls. Choose a label from Assign to Selection. The new label is applied to the selected calls immediately. Choose Add New Call Type to create a new label.
Reject selected calls. Select Reject to relabel the selected calls as Noise.
Convert an entire call type. Use Convert All to change every call of one type to another type in a single step. Choose the current type, choose the new type in To, and click Apply. This applies to all calls of that type in the file, not just those on the current page.




Saving your review
When you are finished, select Save & Close. DeepAcoustics asks where to save the reviewed detections file.






Important



If you made changes and want to keep the original file intact, save under a new file name. Saving under the same name updates the existing file with your changes. If you cancel the save dialog, the changes made in Call Review are not saved.


You can then return to the main window, load the reviewed file, and use Filter Display to step through each call type for a final check.

title: Bioacoustics & Deep Learning
text:
Image-Based Deep Learning in Bioacoustics
The networks and image libraries fueled by image-based deep learning advancements in a variety of industries have allowed image-based approaches to bioacoustic detection and classification to grow extensively to address first terrestrial, and then marine monitoring needs (Kahl et al., 2021; Ghani et al., 2023; Harvey et al., 2024; Hamard et al., 2024). Image-based deep learning methods generally fall within either a binary classification or object detection framework. Binary classification aims to determine whether a specific class of object exists anywhere within an image, whereas object detection, usually leveraging a “You Only Look Once” (YOLO) deep learning architecture, further attempts to locate the object within the image. Both approaches output a class label and confidence score, but in the former these apply to the entire image being analyzed, while in the latter they correspond to a bounding box delineating the signal within the image (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Redmon et al., 2016; Coffey et al., 2019; Shiu et al., 2020). For binary classification tasks, this means that the duration of the audio data used to create the training images must be carefully chosen to frame the signal(s) of interest, and achieving precise temporal resolution of the signals of interest requires processing multiple overlapping images. In object detection, these factors are mitigated through the use of tiling anchor boxes intrinsic in object detection approaches (which effectively function as binary classification models of different sizes and aspect ratios; Amit et al., 2021), which also allows a multi-class approach to signals of varying duration within the same spectrogram (Escobar-Amado et al., 2023; Hamard et al., 2024; Alksne et al., 2026).
Traditional marine acoustic signal processing methods are often quite successful at detecting singular, specific call types (e.g., Mellinger and Clark, 2000; Gillespie et al., 2013). The challenge with many of these algorithms lies in decreased success when applied to highly variable and noisy acoustic environments or to multiple signals of interest simultaneously (Gillespie et al., 2013). Recent performance metrics for deep learning methodologies indicate high levels of detection and consistently low false positive rates. For instance, Padovese et al. (2023) reported a recall of North Atlantic right whale upcalls of 85% and fewer than five false positives per hour. Additionally, the methods used by Kather et al. (2024) for humpback whale detection resulted in an hourly F1-Score of 0.89 with only 5% of context windows labeled incorrectly and a false positive rate of 0.01 per hour. Alksne et al. (2026) obtained further success with multi-class networks for low frequency baleen whales amid variable soundscape conditions. Our research approach to multi-class networks with DeepAcoustics mirrored these low false positive, consistent classification results as well (Alongi et al., in review). These deep learning performance ratings translate to increased capabilities in processing large, highly diverse passive acoustic datasets.



Image-based Object Detection
Image-based object detection methods in bioacoustics leverage spectrograms generated from audio recordings as input for deep learning networks to detect specific calls or signals of interest, such as dolphin whistles. In this process, spectrograms undergo normalization and contrast enhancement to help the model distinguish between calls and background noise. As outlined in Fig. 1, annotations from the audio files are converted into image datastores, which are then used for object detection models in MATLAB. The duration of each spectrogram image is user-defined, with the segment length based on the duration and properties of the target calls of interest. Each spectrogram image is linked to coordinates that identify the location of calls within the image.
To help the model understand not just calls but also noise, spectrograms from audio segments without calls are also used. In these cases, random coordinates mimicking call-like features are applied to these images, allowing the model to learn the characteristics of “Noise” signals. This enables the network to better differentiate between calls and non-call elements in the spectrograms.
Further refinement of the spectrograms is achieved through contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE), which enhances the contrast and normalizes the power spectral densities. Additional variability is introduced by augmenting the spectrograms, adjusting parameters like the Fast-Fourier Transform (FFT) size and overlap. The resulting images are then resized to meet the specific input requirements of the object detection networks, based on available computational resources (Table II). This approach ensures the networks are trained on a diverse range of signals, improving their ability to detect calls across different acoustic environments.



Figure 1: Flow chart of analytical process from raw audio to network selection in DeepAcoustics





YOLO Method of Object-Detection
YOLO (You Only Look Once) is a real-time object detection algorithm that has gained significant attention for its speed and accuracy in identifying objects within images. Unlike traditional methods that use sliding windows or region proposals to detect objects, YOLO treats object detection as a single regression problem, predicting both the class and the bounding box coordinates in a single pass through the network. This streamlined approach allows YOLO to process images much faster, making it well-suited for tasks requiring real-time detection. The algorithm divides the input image into a grid and assigns each grid cell the responsibility of detecting an object if its center falls within that cell. By generating predictions for multiple bounding boxes and their associated confidence scores in one forward pass, YOLO can efficiently detect objects at various scales and positions within the image.
In the context of bioacoustics, YOLO can be adapted to detect specific sounds within spectrogram images. These spectrograms serve as visual representations of sound, and YOLO is trained to recognize the distinct patterns that correspond to specific calls. The model’s ability to quickly process entire images and localize calls within them makes it an effective tool for detecting signals of interest in large datasets. YOLO’s grid-based prediction system allows it to handle overlapping calls and background noise, which is critical in bioacoustic environments where signals can be complex and varied. By training the network on annotated spectrograms, YOLO can learn to differentiate between multiple classes of calls and noise in a single pass, allowing for rapid interpretation of large acoustic datasets.

title: DeepAcoustics Guide and Tutorial
text:
DeepAcoustics Screen



About DeepAcoustics
DeepAcoustics is an open-access, MATLAB-based tool that was modified from a program called DeepSqueak (Coffey et al., 2019). Originally designed for use with ultrasonic calls from rats for neurological studies, our modification of the program has led to an independent version of the software that is optimized to detect calls in noisier, underwater environments. Additional modifications to the classification capabilities are incorporated in DeepAcoustics.
Modifications to DeepAcoustics allowed for a broadened scope that prioritizes underwater acoustic environments and species, while still accommodating in-air terrestrial counterparts. These enhancements extend the tool’s functionality, with key improvements including:

Access to wider bandwidth, including low frequencies that were not previously required for DeepSqueak.
Increased user interactivity in image creation, network training, and multiclass sound detection, ideal for analyzing overlapping call types across bandwidths.
Support for custom duration audio file sizes and integration with Raven selection tables, often used for marine call annotation.
Processing of large acoustic datasets, with the ability to extract date and time stamps directly from file names for streamlined data management.
Ongoing advancements in classification capabilities, ensuring the tool stays at the forefront of bioacoustic research.

These modifications build on the intuitive graphical user interface (GUI) originally developed by Coffey et al., ensuring DeepAcoustics remains accessible to users with varying levels of bioacoustic expertise. It provides a powerful, flexible deep learning tool that simplifies network training and deployment, empowering researchers to tackle both marine and terrestrial acoustic challenges efficiently.






NoteApplicable across species and frequency ranges



DeepAcoustics can be applied to a wide variety of terrestrial and marine species and across a broad range of frequency bandwidths. This guide and tutorial emphasize marine mammals because of our specialization in underwater acoustics, but the same workflow applies to other taxa and sound sources.


For access to this software, please visit the DeepAcoustics repository.



Software Requirements
DeepAcoustics is developed in MATLAB and utilizes the streamlined integration of deep learning modules along with the YOLO (“You Only Look Once”) object detection model, specifically version 4. While this version is not as advanced as Python’s YOLO v9, it offers robust performance for bioacoustic applications. To run DeepAcoustics, the following are required:

MATLAB version R2023b or higher
Deep Learning Toolbox
Computer Vision Toolbox
Signal Processing Toolbox
Parallel Computing Toolbox (for GPU support)
Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox

These requirements ensure optimal performance and efficient handling of deep learning tasks within the software.



GPU Requirements
A GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) is a specialized hardware component designed to handle complex mathematical calculations, especially those related to graphics rendering and parallel processing tasks. While GPUs were originally developed for rendering images and videos in gaming and 3D applications, their architecture has made them highly effective for tasks that involve large-scale matrix and vector operations, which are common in deep learning.
Deep learning tasks, such as training neural networks, require the processing of vast amounts of data and the performance of many computations simultaneously. These tasks involve operations like multiplying large matrices (weights and inputs), calculating gradients, and updating model parameters across multiple layers of the network. CPUs (Central Processing Units) can handle these tasks but are optimized for sequential processing, meaning they are generally slower when performing the parallelized operations deep learning demands. GPUs, on the other hand, are designed to process thousands of operations in parallel, making them much faster for deep learning tasks. This capability is essential when working with large datasets and complex models, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or object detection models like YOLO, where speed and efficiency are crucial. By using GPUs, deep learning models can be trained faster and more efficiently, significantly reducing the time needed for both training and inference, particularly when working with large-scale or real-time applications.
A modern GPU with CUDA support is required for training networks in DeepAcoustics, but is not required for using a trained network model to detect target calls in audio using DeepAcoustics.



Getting Started
This documentation takes users through the features of DeepAcoustics, and then includes a tutorial that users can use for further exploration of this deep learning GUI. Please begin by downloading DeepAcoustics from the GitHub repository below. Then open MATLAB, set the path to the folder you downloaded the software to, and use the word “DeepAcoustics” to call the tool. We recommend using GitHub Desktop to streamline the incorporation of updates to the software.
Access DeepAcoustics








How to Get Help

Software Issues
If you encounter any issues or have questions about DeepAcoustics, please visit the DeepAcoustics Software Issues section. To help us resolve problems efficiently, include the following details when reporting an issue:

MATLAB version you’re using
Platform and OS version (e.g., Windows 11, macOS Ventura)
Steps or code that triggered the issue
What happened vs. what you expected
Any error messages or unusual behavior
Apply the appropriate description in the title (e.g., “Training Bug”)



Discussions
For general inquiries, ideas, or feedback that don’t fit into an issue report, use the Discussions section. This space is ideal for:

Sharing ideas or suggestions for new features
Discussing best practices for using the software effectively
Engaging with other users to ask questions or share insights

Both sections are monitored to ensure you receive timely support and can connect with the broader DeepAcoustics community.

title: GUI Overview
text:
This page walks through the main DeepAcoustics window which is the panel layout you’ll see every time you open the app, including specifics of the File menu options. The general descriptions provided in this and the subsequent informative tabs is reinforced through the step-by-step tutorial exercieses.


Main window layout






A: Title bar / menu bar. The File, Tools, and Help menus. File is covered in detail below; Tools and Help are not yet documented here.
B: Call detail panel. Shows the metadata for whichever call is currently in view including the (Confidence) Score, Status, User ID, Label, Clust Assign, Frequency (KHz), Duration (ms), Slope (KHz/s), Sinuosity, Rel Pwr, and Tonality. Given the original intent of DeepSqueak was detection of ultra-high frequency rat vocalizations and Coffey et al. (2019) intended it as a tool for clustering call types, this per call information is accompanies by a Contour and Waveform displays beneath it. Additional descriptions of these features are available in the classification/clustering section.
C: Neural Networks selector and Save Session. The dropdown chooses which trained network (.mat file) is available in the folder for detection; the blue Save Session button writes your current session (loaded audio, detections, annotations, and settings) to disk.
D: Detect, Load, & Record. Run the active network on the loaded audio (Detect Calls), load existing detections or audio, filter the display, or record new audio.
E: Annotation & Detection. The accept/reject and manual-annotation controls used while reviewing calls. A user can either Accept Call, Reject Call, Draw, Play Call, Draw Label, and Re-Label, each with its keyboard shortcut shown in parentheses.
F: Navigation. Step through calls and pages of the spectrogram display, from single-call steps up to jumping to the first/last call.
G: Settings. Focus and Page duration, Display Settings, Color Map, and the High/Low Color Limit controls that adjust how the spectrogram is rendered.




The File menu
The File menu is where a session usually starts, pointing DeepAcoustics at a trained network and a folder of audio, then loading or saving your work as you go.

Select Network Folder points DeepAcoustics at the folder containing your trained network(s). Once selected, the available networks populate the Neural Networks dropdown (panel C above).
Select Audio Folder points DeepAcoustics at the folder of audio files you want to work with for the current session.
Load Detections loads a previously saved detections file (a .mat file, either one DeepAcoustics produced earlier via Detect Calls, or one saved from a prior session). After you select a file, a dialog lists the call types saved in that file and lets you choose which ones to load:
Note the warning in that dialog: if you save the session afterward without changing the detections file name, it will overwrite the existing file with only the call types you selected here. If you want to keep the full original file intact, save under a new name.
Load Annotations loads a ground-truth annotation file for review or for use in training/testing see Preparing Your Data for the expected format.
Change Playback Rate opens a small dialog for adjusting the speed at which audio is played back during review (default 0.05):
Change Contour Threshold opens a dialog with two settings that control how sensitively the contour overlay is drawn on the spectrogram:

Tonality Threshold (range 0 to 1, default 0.215): how tonal a region of the spectrogram must be before a contour is drawn there.
Amplitude Percentile Threshold (range 0 to 1, default 0.825): the amplitude percentile a pixel must exceed to be included in the contour.

Save Session (Ctrl+S) writes your current session (loaded audio, detections, annotations, and settings) to disk.
Import/Export provides options for importing annotations into DeepAcoustics.


Export to Raven: Exports your annotations from DeepAcoustics into a Raven selection table (a tab-delimited .txt file) that can be opened directly in Raven.
Export to TensorFlow: A two-step process for converting a neural network developed in DeepAcoustics into a TensorFlow model that can be imported into PAMGuard. More details on this process are provided in the following sections.
Export Spectrogram: Saves the spectrogram image currently shown in the DeepAcoustics display panel as a PNG file.
Export Audio: Exports an audio selection as a separate audio file.
Export Excel Log (Call Statistics): Exports an Excel log (.xlsx) of details from your annotations in DeepAcoustics. For each call, the log includes its label, confidence score, and whether it was accepted, along with its begin and end times, duration, frequency measurements (principal, low, high, and peak frequency), slope, sinuosity, mean power, and tonality.
Export to Sonic Visualizer: Exports your annotations as a .csv file of start time, end time, low frequency, high frequency, and label. You can then load this file as an annotation layer in Sonic Visualiser, a free, open-source desktop application from the Centre for Digital Music at Queen Mary University of London for viewing and analyzing audio recordings, including spectrograms and annotation layers.
Import from Raven: The main way to bring annotations into DeepAcoustics from Raven selection tables. You are first prompted to select the Raven table and then the associated audio file. You can also import multiple Raven tables and audio files at once.
Import from Sonic Visualizer, Ultravox, MUPET, and X-BAT: Legacy import tools carried over from DeepSqueak.



The Tools menu
The Tools menu is the most heavily used section of DeepAcoustics. It contains all of the network training, call classification, and review tools.

Network Training is where you create training images and then use them to train detection networks:

Create Detection Network Training Images
Train Detection Network

Call Classification contains the call contour classification components, along with newer VAE and VGG classification tools that are still being developed. It is also where you can view clusters and create t-SNE and UMAP embeddings to visualize how calls group together.
File Management contains utilities for preparing and combining detection files:

Merge Detection Files combines multiple detection files into one.
Add Date/Time adds date and time information to a detection file.
Add Random Noise adds random noise to a file.

Automatic Pruning provides batch tools for cleaning up detection files:

Batch Reject by Threshold rejects all calls that fall below a chosen threshold.

Set Static Box Height (Frequency) sets every bounding box to the same frequency range.

Performance Metrics calculates precision, recall, and other metrics used to evaluate how well a network performs on a test dataset.
Contour Tracing opens a separate GUI window where you can manually adjust the contours generated in the tonality window.
Call Review provides a way to batch review the call detections a network has created, so you can work through a detection file quickly.

title: Importing Data
text:
Once your audio and annotation files are ready (see Preparing Your Data), the next step is to bring them into DeepAcoustics. This page covers two parts of that process: importing a Raven selection table so DeepAcoustics saves it as a detections .mat file, and adjusting the display settings so you can see and navigate your data.


Importing a Raven Selection Table
DeepAcoustics does not work directly from Raven selection tables. Instead, it converts them into its own detections file format (.mat), which is what you load for review, training, and testing.

Open the Raven import. Go to File > Import / Export > Import from Raven.
Answer the Multi-Raven Import prompt. A dialog asks whether you are importing multiple Raven tables and/or audio files, or only one table and its one audio file:

Yes - I have multiple tables and/or audio files: the option you will choose most of the time.
No - I am doing only one table and its one audio file: a legacy option from DeepSqueak, which could only import single audio files. It can still be useful if you are working with one long audio file.


Select the selection table. Navigate to the Raven selection table (.txt) containing your annotations or test data, and select it.
Select the audio folder. DeepAcoustics then asks for the folder containing the audio files that go with the selection table. Select that folder and click OK. DeepAcoustics always asks for this folder during import, even if you selected an audio folder earlier. Additionally, you will be prompted to select an audio file to load. You will be able to navigate to and load the other files, but this is indicating where you want to start in your review:
Save the detections file. Finally, DeepAcoustics asks where to save the new detections file. By default, the file name is built from the name of the first audio file, the total number of audio files, and _Detections.mat. For example:
HYDBBA103OOI_170108-133500_24AudFiles_Detections.mat
If a file with the same name already exists in that location, it will be overwritten.







TipName your .mat files clearly



DeepAcoustics saves several kinds of files with the same .mat extension, including detections files and training image files. Suffixes such as _Detections and _Images help, but it is worth adding a clear prefix or suffix of your own so you can always tell what a file contains. For example, adding Annotations to the name of a file of manually annotated calls (such as Train_Annotations.mat) separates it from a file of detections produced by a network.





Visualizing the Data
Once the detections file is saved, you can load it and adjust the display to suit your calls.

Loading the detections file

Load the detections. Go to File > Load Detections (see GUI Overview) and choose your detections file. If your file has a single call type, it will simply open. If there are multiple call types, a dialog lists the call types in the file and lets you choose which ones to load. See the next section about Annotation Review for how to best use this feature.
Choose a starting audio file. DeepAcoustics asks which audio file to load. This only sets where in the dataset you start; all the other audio files remain available. In most cases, select the first audio file in the folder and click OK.








Important



If you save your session afterward without changing the detections file’s name, DeepAcoustics will overwrite the existing file, keeping only the call types you selected when loading it. To keep the complete original file, save your session under a new file name instead.




Adjusting the display settings
When you first load a detections file, the spectrogram may still use settings from the last file you loaded, or the default settings. For example, if you last reviewed blue whale calls and are now loading dolphin detections, the display will still be set up for blue whales. You will usually need to adjust the controls in the Settings panel before your calls display well.
Focus and Page durations

Focus: sets the duration shown in the upper (focus) spectrogram. A value of around 30 seconds is a good starting point for getting an overall sense of a file. You can then shorten or lengthen it to zoom in or out, depending on your calls and what you want to see.
Page: sets the duration shown in the lower (page) spectrogram panel. It works well to set this to the length of your audio files, for example 600 seconds for a 10-minute file or 300 seconds for a 5-minute file. You can then see where all the annotations fall within the file.

Detections are also marked along the very bottom of the window. The green density plot shows where detections are concentrated within the loaded file.





The controls for the focus and page time scales are adjacent to the color map tools. For both of the focus and page screens, a user can either define a duration to display, or select from a few pre-set settings.





Display Settings
Select Display Settings to open the spectrogram settings dialog. When you click OK, the spectrograms are redrawn with the new settings and the color limits are recalculated.

Frequency Lower Limit (Hz) and Frequency Upper Limit (Hz): the range of frequencies shown on the spectrogram, in Hz. The lower limit must be less than the upper limit, and the highest frequency that can be displayed is half the sampling rate. For example, the example file has a 2000 Hz sampling rate, so the upper limit is set to 1000 Hz.
Spectrogram Units: the units of the values plotted in the spectrogram, which are also shown on the color bar beside it.

Amplitude: the magnitude of each time and frequency bin of the spectrogram (the default).
Power Spectral Density: the power in each bin, normalized by the sampling rate and the window, and shown on a logarithmic (dB) scale. This can make faint calls easier to see against background noise.

Units of Spectrogram Parameters: whether Window Size and NFFT are entered as a number of Samples or as a duration in Seconds. The two are equivalent (seconds = samples ÷ sampling rate). Seconds can be convenient when you work with files at different sampling rates, because the same duration gives the same time resolution.
Window Size: the length of each chunk of audio that is analyzed to create one column of the spectrogram. Longer windows give finer frequency resolution but blur rapid changes in time; shorter windows show timing more sharply but blur frequency. Long, low-frequency tonal calls (such as blue and fin whale calls) generally suit longer windows, while short or fast-changing calls (such as clicks and whistles) suit shorter windows.
Overlap (%): how much each window overlaps the next. Higher overlap produces a smoother spectrogram along the time axis but takes longer to compute. It must be less than 95%.
NFFT: the number of points used in the Fourier transform of each window, which sets the spacing between frequency bins (sampling rate ÷ NFFT). It is usually set equal to the window size. Setting it larger than the window size pads the window with zeros, which smooths the spectrogram’s appearance without adding true frequency resolution.
Auto Window Size: calculates a window size (and sets NFFT to the same value) so that the spectrogram’s pixels are roughly square, based on the current Focus duration, the frequency limits, and the overlap. It is a quick starting point when you aren’t sure what to use. Audio must be loaded first, because the calculation needs the sampling rate.

Color Map and color limits
The spectrogram is drawn by mapping each value (amplitude or power) to a color in the color map, using MATLAB’s color limits:

Low Color Limit: any value at or below this limit is drawn in the lowest (darkest) color of the color map.
High Color Limit: any value at or above this limit is drawn in the highest (brightest) color.
In between: values that fall between the two limits are spread evenly across the colors in between.

When the display is updated, DeepAcoustics sets the starting limits automatically from the spectrogram itself, using the 10th and 90th percentiles of its values. Each click of + or - then moves that limit by 10% of the current range:

Raising the Low Color Limit (+) pushes more of the quieter background into the darkest color, so the background looks darker and calls stand out more.
Lowering the High Color Limit (-) makes more values reach the brightest color, so faint calls appear brighter. If you lower it too far, strong calls saturate and lose detail.
Moving both limits closer together increases the contrast; moving them apart reduces it.

When Spectrogram Units is set to Amplitude, the Low Color Limit cannot go below zero.

Color Map: the set of colors used to draw the spectrogram (for example, inferno). Choose a different color map, or use the button beside it to invert the current one, to find what works best for viewing your data.




Navigating through the data
DeepAcoustics offers several ways to move through your dataset, depending on what you are trying to do:

Audio file selector: at the top of the upper (focus) spectrogram, you can select a different audio file and go straight to it.
Navigation panel: at the bottom of the window, buttons move you to the next or previous call, or forward and back through the spectrogram by a small step or a full page.
File buttons (pink): these move to the next or previous audio file, or to the next or previous audio file that contains a call.
Go to a specific call: in the upper left corner, type an annotation number to jump directly to that call. This is useful for returning to where you left off when reviewing or annotating.

title: Network Architectures, Hyperparameters & Performance Metrics
text:
This page lays out the technical building blocks referenced throughout the rest of the guide: the network architectures DeepAcoustics offers, the hyperparameters you can tune when training one, and the metrics used to evaluate how well a trained network performs. The hands-on, step-by-step process of actually creating training images, training a network, and running performance tests in DeepAcoustics is covered separately under Network Training & Testing; this page is the conceptual reference those steps point back to.


Available architectures
DeepAcoustics offers three pre-trained YOLOv4 backbone architectures. TinyYOLO and CSP-DarkNet-53 are pre-trained on COCO, a segmentation-based database of over 330,000 object images; ResNet-50 is pre-trained on ImageNet, a bounding-box-based database of roughly 1.5 million images.
