TinyYOLO is the lightest and fastest to train, making it the natural starting point for optimizing other settings before moving to the larger architectures. CSP-DarkNet-53 is the largest and most complex of the three, with roughly five times TinyYOLO’s parameter count and an additional detection head. ResNet-50 sits in between, and additionally requires a fixed 224×224 input resolution (TinyYOLO and CSP-DarkNet-53 instead require an input resolution that is a multiple of 32 pixels).ectures. To be added once available.



Key hyperparameters
Training behavior is governed by a handful of settings a user can tune:

Learning rate: controls how large a step the network takes when updating its weights after each training batch. Values of 0.0001, 0.0005, 0.001, and 0.002 have all been tested; too high a rate can cause unstable training, too low can make training impractically slow.
Batch / mini-batch size: the number of training images processed together before each weight update. Values from 16 up to 512 have been tested; larger batches use more GPU memory but can produce more stable gradient estimates.
Epochs: the number of complete passes through the training dataset. Training is typically monitored via a loss curve (below) to judge when additional epochs stop helping.
Optimizer: the algorithm used to update network weights (e.g., sgdm, RMSProp, adam in MATLAB’s implementation); different optimizers can affect convergence speed and stability.
Validation split: the percentage of training data automatically held back each epoch to monitor performance on unseen data during training, rather than supplying a separate validation folder. The reference network used an 18% automatic split.






How to read a training/validation loss curve: both curves falling together (underfitting; more training may help), both low and stable (good fit), or validation loss rising while training loss keeps falling (overfitting; stop near the point where validation loss is lowest).

Anchor boxes
YOLO-family networks don’t draw each bounding box from scratch. Instead, they start from a small set of ready-made box shapes called anchor boxes and learn how to move and stretch the closest shape to fit each call. DeepAcoustics works out the anchor shapes from the bounding boxes in your own training annotations, so they reflect the real shapes of your calls.






Divide the spectrogram into a grid. Every square in the grid looks for calls at the same time, in a single pass through the network.
Start from a few box shapes. Each square has the same set of anchor box shapes, centered on that square. The shapes do not slide or scan across the image.
Move and stretch the closest shape. The square containing the center of a call takes the closest-matching anchor shape and shifts and stretches it to fit the call.
Keep the best box. Every square makes a guess with a confidence score from 0 to 1. Guesses on empty noise score low and are dropped by the confidence threshold. Where several boxes overlap the same call, only the highest-scoring box is kept (a step called non-maximum suppression).


Common questions

How does the network know how to fit a call? It learns from your annotations. During training, each annotated call is assigned to the square containing its center and the closest anchor shape, and the network is corrected based on how closely its adjusted box matches your annotation.
Is there a call in every square? No. Most squares contain only noise and learn to give very low scores. A square only needs to contain the center of a call; its box can extend well beyond the square, and its prediction draws on a much larger area of the image around it.
Where do false positives come from? When a guess on something in the noise (a ship, another species, a mooring sound) looks enough like a call to score above the confidence threshold, it is kept as a detection.



Choosing the number of anchor boxes

Use the mean IoU curve: when you choose Customize during training, DeepAcoustics can plot mean IoU (how well the anchor shapes match your annotated boxes) for 1 to 15 anchors. Choose the number where the curve levels off.
More anchors: a closer starting match for unusually shaped calls and tighter boxes, which helps when call shapes vary a lot (for example, multiclass networks with long and short calls). The cost is more computation and memory and a risk of overfitting; very high counts have crashed training on some machines.
Fewer anchors: faster, but calls far from every shape are harder to fit, which can mean looser boxes or missed calls.
Valid counts: Tiny YOLO and ResNet-50 split the anchors across two detection heads and need an even number; CSP-DarkNet-53 has three heads and needs a multiple of three. DeepAcoustics rounds up if needed. The defaults are 8 (9 for CSP-DarkNet-53).
Comparing architectures: keep the total number of anchors as close as possible (for example, 6 on Tiny YOLO compares to 6 on CSP-DarkNet-53, and 8 compares to 9).
Resolution matters: anchors are calculated at the resized image resolution, so networks trained at different image sizes have different anchors even with the same anchor count.




Variability across training runs
Because random factors (weight initialization, data shuffling, augmentation draws) influence each training run, the same TinyYOLO configuration was trained three independent times in developing the reference network, and each resulting network evaluated separately, to characterize how much performance varies for reasons unrelated to the chosen hyperparameters. This context is useful when comparing two configurations that differ only slightly in a performance metric. A difference smaller than the run-to-run variability isn’t necessarily meaningful.




Performance metrics

Intersection over Union (IoU)
IoU measures how much a predicted bounding box overlaps a ground-truth (manually annotated) box. It is calculated as the area of their overlap divided by the area of their union, so not a straight percentage overlap in boxes. A higher IoU threshold demands tighter overlap and is therefore a stricter detection criterion.





IoU = (area of overlap) / (area of union).

Ground-truth box: a bounding box drawn by a person (an annotation), defined by its position, width, and height on the spectrogram.
Predicted box: a bounding box produced by the network (a detection).
IoU threshold: the minimum IoU a predicted box needs with a ground-truth box to count as a correct detection (a true positive). Below the threshold, it counts as a false positive. You choose this threshold when you run Performance Metrics (see Performance Testing). DeepAcoustics suggests 0.5, a common value in image object detection, but the right threshold is up to you and depends on what you need the detections for.



Precision, recall, and F1-score
DeepAcoustics’ built-in performance evaluation compares network detections against a ground-truth annotation file. Precision, recall, and F1-score are reported with every detection included (a confidence score threshold of 0), and a detection counts as a true positive if its IoU with a ground-truth box of the same call type reaches the IoU threshold you choose.

Precision: the proportion of the network’s detections that were correct (true positives ÷ all detections).
Recall: the proportion of actual annotated calls the network successfully detected (true positives ÷ all ground-truth calls).
F1-score: the harmonic mean of precision and recall, giving equal weight to both and penalizing large gaps between them more than a simple average would.



Average precision (AP) and mean average precision (mAP)
Classification metrics such as precision and recall only ask whether a call is present. Object detection also asks where the call is, so it needs metrics that account for how well the boxes fit:

IoU: how well a predicted box overlaps the annotated box (see above).
Average precision (AP): combines precision and recall at a given IoU threshold into a single number.
Mean average precision (mAP): averages AP across a range of IoU thresholds, summarizing overall detection performance.

A single confidence threshold only tells part of the story. To calculate AP, DeepAcoustics steps the confidence (score) threshold down from the highest score to 0 and records precision and recall at each step, producing a precision-recall curve. IoU is a key part of this calculation, because it decides which detections count as correct at each step. AP is the area under the precision-recall curve, smoothed using interpolation (at each recall level, the precision is taken as the highest precision reached at that recall or higher). An AP of 1 would mean the network found every call with no false positives at every threshold.





An example precision-recall curve in the style of DeepAcoustics’ performance output (example data, not a real evaluation run). Each point is one confidence (score) threshold, colored by its value, and the average precision is shown in the title.
Mean average precision (mAP) repeats the AP calculation at nine IoU thresholds from 0.1 to 0.9 (in steps of 0.1) and averages the results. It therefore captures both how completely calls are detected and how tightly the predicted boxes fit them.
Because the “Noise” class exists only as a training-time workaround for a MATLAB datastore limitation (true negatives can’t otherwise be included in training), performance metrics are not meaningful for, and are not reported on, that class.

title: Performance Testing
text:
Once you have trained a network (see Network Training), the next step is to measure how well it performs. DeepAcoustics does this by running the network on a test dataset that you have already annotated, then comparing the network’s detections against your annotations. The metrics used here (IoU, precision, recall, F1-score, average precision, and mAP) are defined in Performance metrics.


Before You Start

Prepare a ground-truth test file. Annotate a test dataset ahead of time, in Raven or in DeepAcoustics, and convert it into a detections .mat file. If you annotated in Raven, import the selection table as described in Importing Data. The test data should not be part of the data used to train the network, so the results show how the network performs on calls it has never seen.
Name your files clearly. Ground-truth files, network detections, and networks are all .mat files, and detections files all end in _Detections.mat. Give your ground-truth file a name that makes it obvious it contains your verified annotations (for example, HYDDBA105OOI_20170203_Test_Detections.mat).
Select the network folder. Go to File > Select Network Folder and choose the folder where you saved the network you want to evaluate.




Running Performance Metrics

Open the tool. Go to Tools > Performance Metrics.
Select the ground-truth file. Choose your ground-truth detections file, the one containing your verified annotations. You can select more than one file if your test data are split across several.
Choose the call types. Select the call types to load from the ground-truth file. You can choose a single call type to evaluate on its own, or click Select all to evaluate all of them. In this example, all call types are selected.
Select the network. Choose the network .mat file you want to evaluate. This can be any network you have trained, which is why a clear network name matters.
Enter the settings for running the network. The Settings for Running This Network dialog has three settings, all of which can usually be left at 0 (see below). Click OK.
Let the network run. DeepAcoustics runs the network on every audio file in the ground-truth file. A Detecting Calls progress bar appears, along with a progress window for each audio file as it is processed.
Set the true positive threshold. The True Positive Threshold dialog asks for the IoU threshold that a detection must reach to count as correct (see below). Click OK.
Review the results. For each call type, DeepAcoustics displays a precision-recall curve and a P/R Result summary, plus a confusion matrix for all call types (see Understanding the results).
Save the performance metrics file. DeepAcoustics asks where to save the performance metrics (the default name is PerformanceMetrics.mat). We recommend saving it in a dedicated folder and renaming it to include both the test file and the network, for example HYDDBA105OOI_20170203_Test_TinyYOLO_v1_PerformanceMetrics.mat.
Save the network’s detections. DeepAcoustics then asks where to save the detections the network made on the test data. This is a regular detections file that you can load with Load Detections to visually inspect how well the network did, call by call. The default name is built from the name of the last audio file processed and the number of audio files (for example, HYDDBA105OOI_20170203-060000_49AudFiles_Detections.mat), so consider renaming it to include the network name.





Settings for Running This Network
This dialog is partly a legacy feature. The frequency limits are taken automatically from the network, so only three settings remain, and all three can normally stay at their defaults of 0:

Total Analysis Length (Seconds; 0 = Full Duration): how much of the test audio to analyze, in seconds. Use 0 to analyze all of it. A shorter length, such as 60 seconds, can be useful for a quick trial run on a long test file.
Score Threshold (0-1): the minimum confidence score a detection needs to be kept. The default of 0 keeps every detection, regardless of its confidence score, so the full precision-recall curve can be calculated. Set it higher (for example, 0.5) only if you want to keep just the more confident detections.
Append Date to FileName (1 = yes): enter 1 to add the date and time of the run to the name of the saved detections file. The default is 0 (no date).




True Positive Threshold
The Threshold for overlap (0-1) that counts as a true positive is the IoU threshold: how much a detection’s bounding box must overlap the matching ground-truth box to count as a true positive (see Intersection over Union (IoU)). The default is 0.5, a common value in image object detection. The right threshold is up to you and depends on what you need the network’s detections for. For example:

0.1, detecting the call at all: a detection counts as correct if its box overlaps the call even a little. Use this when you mainly want to know whether the network finds calls, not how well it boxes them.
0.5, detecting the call moderately well: a detection counts as correct only if its box covers a good part of the call.
0.9, boxing almost all of the call: a detection counts as correct only if its box closely matches the annotated box. Use this when tight boxes matter, for example if you plan to take measurements from the detections.

The example results below use 0.1.

This threshold is used for the true positives, false positives, false negatives, precision, recall, F1-score, average precision, and confusion matrix. The mAP is always calculated across IoU thresholds from 0.1 to 0.9, regardless of this setting.



Understanding the Results

Precision-recall curve and P/R Result
DeepAcoustics produces a precision-recall curve and a P/R Result summary for every call type the network was trained on (except Noise), even if that call type does not occur in the test file. Call types that are not in the test file will have empty curves and missing values.
Precision-recall curve: each point is one confidence (score) threshold. Moving from left to right, the threshold is lowered, so more detections are included: recall rises and precision usually falls. The color of each point shows its score threshold (yellow = high, dark blue = low). The title shows the call type and its average precision (rounded to one decimal place). See Average precision (AP) and mean average precision (mAP) for how to interpret the curve.
P/R Result: these values are calculated at a score threshold of 0, meaning every detection the network made is included:

# True Positives: detections that match a ground-truth call of the same call type, with an IoU at or above the true positive threshold.
# False Positives: detections of this call type that do not match a ground-truth call of the same type. This includes detections on noise and detections that matched a call but gave it the wrong call type.
# of False Negatives: ground-truth calls of this call type that the network missed (or detected with the wrong call type).
Precision: true positives ÷ all detections of this call type.
Recall: true positives ÷ all ground-truth calls of this call type.
F-Score: the F1-score, the balance between precision and recall: 2 × (precision × recall) ÷ (precision + recall).
Average Prec: the average precision at the true positive (IoU) threshold you entered, shown in parentheses.
mAP: the mean average precision across IoU thresholds from 0.1 to 0.9, in steps of 0.1.


For example, for the fin whale 20 Hz calls, with an IoU threshold of 0.1: 269 true positives, 80 false positives, and 19 false negatives give a precision of 269 ÷ 349 = 0.7708, a recall of 269 ÷ 288 = 0.9340, and an F-score of 0.8446. The average precision is 0.9050, and the mAP is 0.3614. The much lower mAP shows that many detections find the call but do not box it tightly enough to pass the stricter IoU thresholds.


Confusion matrix
DeepAcoustics also displays a confusion matrix showing how the network’s call types compare with the ground truth, at the true positive threshold you entered. It is most useful for multiclass networks, where it shows which call types are being confused with each other:

Rows are the true call types (from the ground-truth file), and columns are the call types the network predicted.
The diagonal shows correct detections (true positives).
Off-diagonal cells show calls detected with the wrong call type. For example, in the test run, 3 fin whale 20 Hz calls were detected as 18 Hz.
The “unmatched” column shows ground-truth calls the network missed (false negatives).
The “unmatched” row shows detections that did not match any ground-truth call (false positives on noise).
The row and column summaries at the edges show each row and column as percentages, so you can see at a glance which call types are most often missed or confused.


Detections the network labeled as Noise are not counted as calls and are added to the unmatched category.




What’s in the Performance Metrics File
The performance metrics .mat file stores everything needed to review or report the results later. You can load it into MATLAB to look at the values directly.
Run information







Variable
Description




NetName, NetPath
The file name and folder of the network that was evaluated.


PathToDet
The full path to the ground-truth detections file used for testing.



Results for each call type
These variables have one value per call type, in the same order as the call types stored in the network (detector.ClassNames in the network file). This list includes Noise and any call types that are not in the test file, which have missing (NaN) values.







Variable
Description




numTrueDets
The number of ground-truth calls of each call type in the test file.


numDets
The number of detections the network made for each call type.


numTP, numFP, numFN
The numbers of true positives, false positives, and false negatives, at a score threshold of 0.


prec, recall, fscore
Precision, recall, and F1-score, at a score threshold of 0.


avgprec
Average precision at the true positive (IoU) threshold you entered.


mAP
Mean average precision across IoU thresholds from 0.1 to 0.9.


precvec, recallvec
The precision and recall values that make up each precision-recall curve, one pair of values per score threshold. These can be used to re-plot the curves.



Detailed results







Variable
Description




results
A table of every detection the network made, with its bounding box (Box), confidence score (Scores), and call type (Label).


confMat, confusionClassNames
The confusion matrix counts and the call type names for its rows and columns (including “unmatched”).


odMetrics
MATLAB’s full object detection metrics at the true positive threshold you entered.


odMetricsmAP
MATLAB’s full object detection metrics across IoU thresholds from 0.1 to 0.9, used to calculate the mAP.



For example, in the test run, numTrueDets shows 148 fin whale 18 Hz calls, 288 fin whale 20 Hz calls, 36 blue whale A calls, and 64 blue whale B calls in the ground-truth file, and the confusion matrix accounts for every one of them as either a correct detection, a call detected with the wrong call type, or a missed call.

title: Network Training & Testing
text:
Once your data are annotated and reviewed, you can train a deep learning network to find those calls for you. This section walks through the full process, from turning your annotations into training images to running a finished network on new audio. The architectures, settings, and performance metrics referred to throughout are explained in Architectures, Hyperparameters & Metrics.


The Workflow

Creating Training Images: convert your annotated audio into spectrogram images, each paired with the bounding boxes of the calls it contains. The spectrogram and image settings you choose here have a large effect on how well the network performs.
Network Training: train a detection network on those images. You choose the base network (Tiny YOLO, CSP-DarkNet-53, or ResNet-50, which are pre-trained, or a blank ResNet-50 that is still being evaluated), the anchor boxes, and the training settings, and watch the training and validation loss as the network learns.
Performance Testing: run the trained network on a separate, annotated test dataset and compare its detections with your annotations, using precision, recall, F1-score, average precision, mAP, and a confusion matrix.
Network Deployment: use the network to detect calls in new audio, add the date and time to each detection, and export the detections to a Raven selection table.




Before You Start

Annotate thoroughly. DeepAcoustics adds noise examples automatically from the parts of your audio outside the annotation boxes, so every call of interest in an annotated file needs to be boxed. See Preparing Your Data and Annotation Review.
Keep test data separate. Set aside annotated audio that is not used for training, so performance testing shows how the network handles calls it has never seen.
Organize your folders. Decide where your training images, image tables, networks, and results will be saved before you start. The image table stores the location of every training image, so the images should not be moved afterward.
Keep track of your settings. You will likely train several networks with different settings before finding the one that works best. Recording the settings and test results for each network makes them easy to compare. The tutorial data includes a spreadsheet template for this.







TipTraining is an iterative process



There is rarely a single right set of settings. Start with a fast architecture such as Tiny YOLO, test the network, change one setting at a time, and compare the results. The Tutorial takes you through each of these steps with example data.
